ibadan: Ibadan is the capital of Oyo State, about 120 kilometres inland northeast of Lagos. Its name is said to come from Eba-Odan, meaning by the edge of the meadow. The site is a forest of several ranges of hills between 160 and 275 metres high, which offered strategic defence, and its position at the fringe of the forest made it a trading point between forest and grassland. The principal inhabitants are Yoruba, with communities from other parts of Nigeria. Parts of the city's old protective walls still stand.

Ibadan came into existence in 1829, during a period of turmoil in Yorubaland in which older cities such as Old Oyo, Ijaye and Owu disappeared and newer ones such as Abeokuta, New Oyo and Ibadan arose. According to local historians Lagelu founded it, at first as a war camp for warriors from Oyo, Ifẹ and Ijebu. It began as a military state and kept that character until the last decade of the 19th century. Historians have called it a military republic, unlike most Yoruba cities with hereditary kingship; four chiefs governed it, three of whose offices were open to all freeborn males and one reserved for women.

Warriors were the dominant class and military success offered a path of advancement, which earned it the derision of other Yoruba. Between the 1860s and 1890s it was the centre of an empire over much of northern and eastern Yorubaland, nicknamed idi-Ibon, gun base.

Refugees came in large numbers from northern Oyo after raids by Fula warriors, and in 1840 Ibadan's armies decisively defeated an attempt by the Sokoto Caliphate to expand southwards. David and Anna Hinderer of the Church Missionary Society arrived in 1853 and founded a mission and the city's first Western schools. In 1893 the area became a British protectorate after a treaty signed by Fijabi, the Baale of Ibadan, with the acting Governor of Lagos Colony, George C. Denton, on 15 August. After a small rubber boom from 1901 to 1913, cocoa became the main product. Ibadan was made headquarters of the Western Provinces in 1939.

At independence in 1960 Ibadan was the most populous city in Nigeria and the second most populous in Africa after Cairo. Its metropolitan area now has some four million people. The University of Ibadan was founded in 1948 as a college of the University of London and became autonomous in 1962. The University College Hospital was the first teaching hospital in Nigeria. Western Nigeria Television, begun at Ibadan in 1959, was the first television station in Africa. Cocoa House at Dugbe was the first skyscraper in West Africa, and Bower's Tower, built in 1936, stands on Oke Aàre.
ibaraki-prefecture: Ibaraki lies on Japan's eastern Pacific coast and borders Fukushima Prefecture to the north, Tochigi to the north-west, Saitama to the south-west and Chiba to the south. Its northern third is mountainous, with the Tsukuba Mountains at the centre, but most of it is a flat plain with many lakes, part of the Kantō Plain. It has Lake Kasumigaura, the second-largest lake in Japan, and the Tone River, the second longest in the country. In the 17th century the Tokugawa shogunate diverted the Edo River's source to the Tone to protect Edo from flooding.

Humans are believed to have lived in the area around the time of the ash deposit from the Aira Caldera about 24,000 years ago. During the Asuka period the provinces of Hitachi and Fusa were created, and Fusa was later divided, among others, into Shimōsa Province. In the 14th century Kitabatake Chikafusa made Oda Castle his field headquarters for over a year and wrote the Jinnō Shōtōki there.

In the Edo period one of the three Tokugawa houses descended from Tokugawa Ieyasu settled in the Mito Domain, in Hitachi Province, and became known as the Mito Tokugawa. In 1657 Tokugawa Mitsukuni, head of the domain, commissioned the Dai Nihonshi, a history of Japan, and the Mito school of learning grew from it. In 1833 Tokugawa Nariaki began breeding black cattle at Mito. During the Meiji Restoration the old provinces were converted or merged into prefectures: the province became Ibaraki in 1871, and in 1875 the prefecture reached its present size by taking in districts of the former Shimōsa Province.

Mito is the capital and largest city, and other major cities are Tsukuba, Hitachi and Hitachinaka. The prefecture has 2,828,086 people in 2023. Hitachi, Ltd. was founded at Sukegawa, in Hitachi, in 1910, and Tsukuba is a research and academic city with dozens of institutes. Agriculture is important, with melons, pears and peppers among its products, and Mito is known for nattō and for Kairakuen, one of the Three Great Gardens of Japan, with over 3,000 plum trees. Morihei Ueshiba, founder of Aikido, spent the later part of his life at Iwama, now part of Kasama, where his shrine and dojo remain.
iberia: The Iberian Peninsula is the westernmost of the three major southern European peninsulas, with the Italian and Balkan peninsulas. The Pyrenees separate it from the rest of continental Europe, and the Strait of Gibraltar divides its southern tip at Tarifa from the northwest coast of Africa. Its area is about 583,254 square kilometres, and its major rivers, the Ebro, Douro, Tagus, Guadiana and Guadalquivir, flow through wide valleys between mountain systems.

The name goes back to the River Ebro, called Ibēros in Greek and Hiberus in Latin. The Ebro Treaty of 226 BCE between Rome and Carthage set the limit of Carthaginian interest at that river. Greek geographers used Iberia for the land this side of it, and Roman writers used Hispania and Hiberia as synonyms. The modern phrase Iberian Peninsula was coined in 1823 by the French geographer Jean-Baptiste Bory de Saint-Vincent.

People of the genus Homo have lived on the peninsula for at least 1.2 million years, as remains at the Atapuerca sites show. Around 2800 to 2700 BCE the Beaker culture probably arose among copper-using communities of the Tagus estuary and spread through western Europe. Bronze Age cultures such as Los Millares and El Argar developed from about 1800 BCE. By the Iron Age the peninsula held Celtic and pre-Celtic peoples, the Iberians of the east and south, and the Aquitanian cultures in the west of the Pyrenees. Phoenician merchants from Tyre founded the trading colony of Gadir, and they traded with the metal-rich community known as Tartessos.

Roman troops first occupied the peninsula in 218 BCE, during the Second Punic War against the Carthaginians, and after 197 BCE the Romans divided the Mediterranean coast and the Guadalquivir valley into Hispania Ulterior and Hispania Citerior. Celtiberian and Lusitanian resistance led to wars in the 2nd century BCE. In the early 5th century the Suebi, Vandals and Alans occupied the peninsula, and the Visigoths then took all of it, absorbing the Suebi kingdom in 584–585. Umayyad conquest followed.

In the 15th and 16th centuries Iberian expansion began a new age. The Portuguese established routes to Asia, and Spain created a vast empire in the Americas, with Seville at the centre of the transatlantic bullion trade. Jews and Moriscos were banished, and roughly 300,000 Moriscos were expelled from Spain in 1609–1614.

The peninsula is divided between most of Spain and Portugal, the microstate of Andorra, the British territory of Gibraltar and a small part of France. Its population is roughly 53 million, and its largest cities are Madrid, Barcelona and Lisbon. Apart from Basque, which is of unknown origin, all its languages descend from Vulgar Latin.
ibn-arabi: Ibn Arabi was born in the Taifa of Murcia, in what is now south-eastern Spain, in 1165, and was named Muhammad. His father served in the army of Ibn Mardanish, ruler of Murcia. After Murcia fell to the Almohad Caliphate in 1172 and Ibn Mardanish was killed in battle, the father pledged allegiance to the Almohad caliph, and the family moved to Seville to serve the new ruler. Ibn Arabi grew up at the ruling court and received military training.

As a teenager he had a first vision, and the philosopher and judge Ibn Rushd, Averroes, asked to meet him. Ibn Arabi said that he learned from this meeting to tell formal knowledge from the unveiling of insight into the nature of things, and he then took up Sufism.

He left al-Andalus for the first time at 28, reaching Tunis in 1193, and crossed from Gibraltar for the last time in 1200, after a vision that told him to go east. He reached Mecca for the pilgrimage in 1202 and lived there three years, beginning there his largest work, the Meccan Illuminations. He then travelled through Syria, Palestine, Iraq and Anatolia, entering Baghdad in 1205.

In 1223 he chose Damascus as his final home and spent his last years teaching and writing there. He composed The Bezels of Wisdom in 1229 and finished two drafts of the Meccan Illuminations, in 1231 and 1238. About 850 works are attributed to him, of which around 700 are thought authentic and over 400 survive.

Ibn Arabi is known as the first to set out explicitly the doctrine of waḥdat al-wujūd, the unity of being, which holds that everything in the universe manifests a single reality, which he called Absolute Being. He distinguished rational knowledge, which he held to be fallible, from experiential knowledge, which he called dhawq, and from divine knowledge, which he believed was given to prophets and their spiritual heirs.

He died on 16 November 1240 and was buried on Qasiyun Hill in Damascus. His teaching spread quickly through the Islamic world, carried by the Sufi orders and by works in Persian, Turkish and Urdu, and he came to be called Shaykh al-Akbar.
ibn-battuta: All that is known of Ibn Battuta's life comes from the account of his travels. It records that he was of Arabised Berber descent and was born into a family of Islamic legal scholars, known as qadis, in Tangier on 24 February 1304, under the Marinid dynasty. His family belonged to a Berber clan called the Lawata. As a young man he probably studied at a Sunni Maliki school, the dominant form of education in North Africa at the time.

On 14 June 1325, aged 21, he set out from Tangier on the hajj to Mecca, a journey that would ordinarily take sixteen months. He did not return to Morocco for 24 years. He travelled overland along the North African coast through Tlemcen, Béjaïa and Tunis, usually joining a caravan for safety, and reached Alexandria in the early spring of 1326. After his third pilgrimage to Mecca he decided to seek employment with Muhammad bin Tughluq, the Sultan of Delhi, and went by way of Anatolia, where members of the fityan associations of young artisans welcomed him in more than 25 towns.

He left Quanzhou in 1346 and reached Damascus in 1348, where he learned that his father had died 15 years earlier. He saw the Black Death in Syria, Palestine and Egypt, and he was back in Tangier in 1349, only to find that his mother had also died. In 1350 he went to al-Andalus, and in 1352 he crossed the Sahara by caravan from Sijilmasa, by way of the salt mines of Taghaza, to Oualata, which had recently become part of the Mali Empire.

After he came home in 1354, the Marinid ruler Abu Inan Faris suggested that he dictate an account of his journeys, which he did in Arabic to the scholar Ibn Juzayy. It is known as the Rihla and is the only source for his travels. He seems to have kept no notes, and Ibn Juzayy copied descriptions of Damascus, Mecca, Medina and Palestine from earlier travellers without acknowledging them. Modern scholars doubt that Ibn Battuta visited every place he describes. In 2010 Tim Mackintosh-Smith reported manuscripts of Islamic law at Al-Azhar University copied by Ibn Battuta in Damascus in 1326, which support the Rihla's date for his stay in Syria.
ibn-khaldun: Abd al-Rahman ibn Khaldun was born in Tunis in 1332 into an upper-class Andalusian family of Yemeni Arab descent, the Banu Khaldun, whose eponymous ancestor had settled first in Carmona and then in Seville. His first and most influential teacher was his father, under whom he studied the Islamic and the rational sciences. He also learned from Moroccan and Tunisian scholars and from Andalusian exiles in Tunis, studying Quranic recitation, Maliki law, hadith and poetry, and while still young he became a hafiz. His autobiography is described as the most detailed in medieval Muslim literature, though it lacks many personal details.

At 20 Ibn Khaldun began his political career in the chancellery of the Tunisian ruler Ibn Tafrakin as seal-bearer. Unhappy with this politically meaningless position, he followed his teacher al-Abili to Fez, where the Marinid sultan Abu Inan Fares I made him a writer of royal proclamations. He schemed against his employer and in 1357 received a prison sentence of 22 months, which ended with Abu Inan's death in 1358. He travelled through Fez, Granada and Tlemcen, repeatedly changing roles, and arrived in Cairo in 1380.

In 1384 the sultan Barquq made him professor of the Qamhiyyah Madrasah and grand qadi of the Maliki school. His efforts to reform abuses in the administration of justice met resistance, and within a year he resigned. A ship carrying his wife and children sank off Alexandria that year. He was called to the Maliki judgeship six times and never held it long.

His best-known book is the Muqaddimah, the Introduction, which he says he wrote in six months. It is the first book of the Kitab al-Ibar, begun as a history of the Berbers and expanded into a universal history in seven books. He departed from the classical style of Arab historians by synthesising multiple, sometimes contradictory sources without citations. His method had very few followers in his own time, but Ottoman historians such as Katip Celebi took up his theory of the rise and fall of empires in the 17th century. Europe first learned of him in 1697 through a biography in d'Herbelot's Bibliothèque Orientale, and the complete Arabic edition of the Muqaddimah appeared in 1858.
ibn-saud: Ibn Saud was born in Riyadh, the fourth child and third son of Abdul Rahman bin Faisal, one of the last rulers of the Emirate of Nejd, the second Saudi state, a tribal sheikhdom centred on Riyadh. The Al Saud family had been a power in central Arabia for about 130 years. The family's long-term rivals, led by Muhammad bin Abdullah Al Rashid, conquered Riyadh when Ibn Saud was a boy, and the family took refuge with the Al Murrah, a Bedouin tribe, and then settled in Kuwait for nearly a decade, where he developed a rapport with the ruler Mubarak Al Sabah. His paternal aunt, Jawhara bint Faisal, told him of his ancestors' deeds and helped persuade him to return to Nejd.

He reconquered Riyadh in 1902, and many former supporters of the House of Saud rallied to him. Over the next two years his forces recaptured almost half of Nejd from the Rashidis. On 15 June 1904 combined Ottoman and Rashidi forces defeated him heavily, but he waged a guerrilla war on the Ottomans and in February 1905 they named him qaimmaqam of southern Nejd. His victory at Rawdat Muhanna ended the Ottoman presence in Nejd and Qassim by the end of October 1906.

Over three decades his conquests made him ruler of nearly all of central and northern Arabia. He consolidated control over Najd in 1921 and conquered the Hejaz in 1925, and in 1932 his dominions became the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. He signed a friendship and cooperation pact with Britain in 1915. In the Saudi-Yemeni War of 1934 the Treaty of Taif confirmed his sovereignty over Asir, Jazan and Najran. Oil was discovered in 1938, after he granted a concession in 1933.

He kept Saudi Arabia neutral in the Second World War. On 14 February 1945 he met the American president Franklin D. Roosevelt aboard USS Quincy on the Great Bitter Lake, a meeting that laid the basis of later relations between the two countries. He fathered almost one hundred children, including 45 sons. He died in his sleep at Shubra Palace in Ta'if on 9 November 1953, with Prince Faisal at his side, and was buried in Riyadh next to his sister Noura. His sons have succeeded him as kings.
ibn-taymiyya: Ibn Taymiyya was born on 22 January 1263 in Harran, to a family of Hanbali scholars. His father held the Hanbali chair in Harran and later at the Umayyad Mosque in Damascus. In 1269, aged seven, he left Harran with his father and three brothers, and the city was destroyed in the Mongol invasion that followed. The family settled in Damascus, under Mamluk rule. After his father died in 1284 he took over the Sukkariyya madrasa and began to lecture on hadith.

During the Mongol invasions of Syria, from 1299 to 1303, Ibn Taymiyya declared the Ilkhanid regime unbelieving because it ruled by the Mongol Yassa code rather than sharia. He urged resistance in Damascus, rebuked those who fled, and issued fatwas making jihad against the Mongols a duty. His third fatwa, of 1303, is sometimes called his best known. He also issued a ruling for jihad against the Shia of Kisrawan.

He was imprisoned several times for conflicts with the jurists and theologians of his day. His creedal work Al-Aqidah Al-Waasitiyyah, which held that God should be described as the Qur'an and hadith describe him, drew four hearings in 1305-1306. After a debate at the Citadel of Cairo on 8 April 1306 he was jailed on the charge of anthropomorphism until 25 September 1307. He returned to Damascus on 28 February 1313, where he taught Ibn Qayyim al-Jawziyya.

His treatise on journeys to the tombs of prophets and saints condemned the cult of saints. For it he was imprisoned in the Citadel of Damascus on 18 July 1326, and the sultan forbade him to issue fatwas. He fell ill in early September 1328 and died on 26 September, aged 65. Thousands came to pay their respects, and he was buried in the cemetery of the Sufis. Many hold that portrayals of him as hostile to Sufism are inaccurate, since he praised many Sufi masters and belonged to the Qadiriyya order.

His writings influenced Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab and the Salafi movement, and in the 20th century his anti-Mongol fatwas were taken up by Islamist thinkers such as Sayyid Qutb, who applied them to the governments of their own day.
ignatius-of-loyola: Ignatius was born Íñigo López de Oñaz y Loyola, probably on 23 October 1491, in the castle of Loyola in Azpeitia, Gipuzkoa. He was the youngest of thirteen children of parents from the minor nobility, and his mother died soon after his birth. He became a page in the household of Juan Velázquez de Cuéllar, treasurer of the kingdom of Castile, and in 1509 entered the service of Antonio Manrique de Lara, Duke of Nájera. On 20 May 1521, at the Battle of Pamplona, a cannonball ricocheting off a wall broke his right leg. Several operations left it shorter than the other, and he limped for the rest of his life.

While recovering he asked for romances of chivalry, but the castle had none, and his sister-in-law Magdalena de Araoz brought him lives of Christ and the saints. Ludolph of Saxony's De Vita Christi struck him most, and its method of imagining oneself at a Gospel scene shaped his later meditation. In March 1522 he visited Montserrat and hung his sword and dagger at the Virgin's altar. He then lived for about a year at Manresa, begging and praying in a cave, where he formulated the basis of his Spiritual Exercises. In September 1523 he reached the Holy Land, but the Franciscans sent him back.

He studied at Alcalá in 1526-1527, where the Inquisition questioned him because he preached without a degree in theology, and then at the University of Paris, adopting the name Ignatius. There six fellow students joined him, among them Francis Xavier, Diego Laynez and Peter Faber. With them he founded the Society of Jesus and became its first Superior General. He aimed it at missionary work and teaching and added a fourth vow of obedience to the Pope to the usual vows of chastity, obedience and poverty.

Ignatius died on 31 July 1556. His method of spiritual formation, recorded in the Spiritual Exercises of 1548, became known as Ignatian spirituality. The Jesuits were instrumental in leading the Counter-Reformation. He was beatified in 1609 and canonised on 12 March 1622, and his feast day is 31 July. He is patron saint of the Basque provinces of Gipuzkoa and Biscay and of the Society of Jesus, and in 1922 Pope Pius XI declared him patron of all spiritual retreats.
ignaz-semmelweis: Ignaz Semmelweis was born on 1 July 1818 in the Tabán neighbourhood of Buda, the fifth of ten children of a prosperous grocer family. His father József Semmelweis ran a wholesale business for spices and consumer goods, and his mother was Teréz Müller. Ignaz began studying law at the University of Vienna in the autumn of 1837 but switched to medicine and received his doctorate in 1844. Having failed to win a post in internal medicine, he specialised in obstetrics.

On 1 July 1846 Semmelweis became assistant to Professor Johann Klein in the First Obstetrical Clinic of the Vienna General Hospital. Its maternal mortality from puerperal fever was about 10 per cent, against under 4 per cent in the Second Clinic, and women begged not to be admitted to the First. His breakthrough came in 1847 after the death of his friend Jakob Kolletschka, who was pricked by a student's scalpel during an autopsy and showed a pathology like that of the dying women. Semmelweis concluded that he and his students carried cadaverous particles on their hands from the autopsy room to patients, and he introduced hand washing in chlorinated lime solutions.

Klein did not extend his term, and Semmelweis had to leave the clinic on 20 March 1849. On 20 May 1851 he took an unpaid post heading the obstetric ward of the Szent Rókus Hospital in Pest, where from 1851 to 1855 only eight of 933 mothers died of childbed fever. His book Etiology, Concept and Prophylaxis of Childbed Fever appeared in 1861.

His claim that the disease had a single cause, a lack of cleanliness, ran against the doctrine of the four humours, and he could not give a theoretical explanation. Some doctors were offended by the suggestion that their hands were unclean. After unfavourable reviews of his book he wrote open letters that were polemical and offensive. In 1865 he was committed to the provincial asylum at Döbling and died there on 13 August 1865, 14 days later, of septic shock, possibly after a beating by guards.
His practice won wide acceptance only years later, when Louis Pasteur's germ theory gave it an explanation and Joseph Lister developed antiseptic surgery. He is called the saviour of mothers.
ile-de-france: The Île-de-France lies in the north-central part of France and covers 12,012 square kilometres, about 2 per cent of metropolitan French territory. The Seine flows through the middle of the region, with tributaries including the Marne, the Oise and the Epte, and the outer parts remain largely rural. Despite the name, which means Island of France, the region is not an island. The island may be the land between the Oise, the Marne and the Seine, or the Île de la Cité, where the royal palace and cathedral stood, or the lands under the direct rule of the kings of the Capetian dynasty, an island in a sea of feudal territories.

The Parisii, a sub-tribe of the Celtic Senones, inhabited the area from about the middle of the 3rd century BCE, and the Romans conquered it in 52 BCE. Saint Denis, the first Bishop of Paris, introduced Christianity in the middle of the 3rd century CE; according to legend he was beheaded on the hill later called Montmartre. Clovis, the first Merovingian king, made Paris his capital in 508. Vikings sacked the Île de la Cité in 845, but the successful defence of Paris in the siege of 885-86 established its strategic importance. In 987 Hugh Capet, Count of Paris, was elected King of the Franks.

The kings hunted in the game-filled forests of the region and built palaces, most notably Fontainebleau and Versailles, which from the time of Louis XIV to the French Revolution was the official residence of the kings and the seat of government. The name Île-de-France came to mean the territory of Paris and the surrounding province, administered directly by the king. The revolution abolished the royal provinces and divided them into departments. In 1959, under President Charles de Gaulle, a new region of six departments, roughly the historic one, was created, and on 6 May 1976 it was renamed Île-de-France.

Île-de-France is the most populous of France's eighteen regions, with over 12 million residents, and contains the capital, Paris. It is made up of eight departments: Paris, Essonne, Hauts-de-Seine, Seine-Saint-Denis, Seine-et-Marne, Val-de-Marne, Val-d'Oise and Yvelines. Beyond Paris it holds historic sites including the palaces of Versailles and Fontainebleau.
ili-river: The Ili is a river of north-western China and south-eastern Kazakhstan, 1,439 kilometres long including its source river the Tekes, of which 815 kilometres are in Kazakhstan. It rises from the Tekes and Künes rivers in the eastern Tian Shan and drains the basin between the Tian Shan and the Borohoro Mountains. It ends in Lake Balkhash, where it forms a large delta of about 8,000 square kilometres between the Saryesik-Atyrau and Taukum deserts. The name is usually taken from the Mongolian il, meaning open or clear, in reference to the river's wide central valley, although other derivations from Persian and Uyghur have been proposed.

The river appears in the Turkic dictionary of Mahmud al-Kashgari, written in 1072-74, which says that the Turkic tribes of the Yaghma, Tokhsi and Chiglig lived on its banks and that Turkic countries regarded it as their Jayhoun, their Amu Darya. In 638 the Ili River treaty formalised the division of the Western Turkic Kaganate (552-638) into the Nushibi and the Dulu and made the river the border between the two states.

The upper valley, on the Chinese side, was the stronghold of the Qing administration in Xinjiang in the late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Russia occupied it from 1871, after the rebellion of Yaqub Beg, until the Treaty of Saint Petersburg of 1881. Its main city, Yining, was long known by the river's name, written Ili, until the early 1900s. The Xibe people, many of whom live in the Qapqal county on the southern bank, resettled there in the eighteenth century as part of the Manchu garrison.

On the Kazakh side the region drained by the river is known as Zhetysu in Kazakh and Semirechye in Russian, both meaning Seven Rivers. Twenty kilometres downstream stands Tamgaly-Tas, a protected site of rock drawings, and the Kapshagay hydroelectric power plant was built near Kapchagay between 1965 and 1970. An area of 9,766 square kilometres in the delta is a Ramsar site, with 427 species of plants and 345 species of animals. Until 1948 the delta was a refuge of the Caspian tiger.
iliad: The Iliad is one of two major surviving ancient Greek epic poems attributed to Homer, the other being the Odyssey. It is divided into 24 books, is written in dactylic hexameter and has 15,693 lines in its standard edition. It was likely composed in Homeric Greek, a literary mixture of Ionic Greek and other dialects, in the late 8th or early 7th century BCE, and its reflection in art and literature shows that it existed before 630 BCE. Its composition, historicity and authorship are extensively debated as the Homeric Question, as is whether the poems were composed independently and whether they survived through an oral or also a written tradition.

The poem is set towards the end of the Trojan War, a ten-year siege of Troy by a coalition of Mycenaean Greek states, and centres on Achilles, whose wrath, mēnis, the poem's first word, drives the narrative. After nine years of fighting, Agamemnon, king of Mycenae, takes the captive Chryseis, and Achilles takes Briseis. Agamemnon's refusal to return Chryseis to her father, a priest of Apollo, brings a plague on the Achaeans, and when Agamemnon seizes Briseis, Achilles withdraws from the fighting.

Patroclus then fights in Achilles's armour and is killed, and Achilles returns to battle and kills the Trojan prince Hector. The poem does not depict the fall of Troy or mention the Trojan Horse, which come from later sources. The Olympian gods aid favoured warriors and cities and intervene in personal disputes, and its themes include glory, fate and pride. In the last book Achilles and Priam share food and grief and agree a truce of twelve days for Hector's burial.

The ancient Greeks esteemed the Iliad highly and used it and the Odyssey as the basis of education. Professional reciters known as rhapsodes performed it at festivals such as the Panathenaia. By the end of the fifth century BCE both poems were widely known, and in the late fifth century it was the sign of a man of standing to be able to recite them by heart.

Later writers drew on it: Shakespeare used it as a source for Troilus and Cressida, and George Chapman published his English translation in instalments from 1598, in a long-line ballad metre that quickly became a classic of English poetry. More than 2,000 manuscripts of Homer survive.
ilkhanate: The Ilkhanate arose in the south-western territories of the Mongol Empire and was known to the Mongols as the Hülegü Ulus, the people or state of Hülegü. Its realm was officially called the Land of Iran, Irān-zamin. After Genghis Khan declared war on the Anushtegin dynasty of Khwarazm in 1219, the Mongols overran Iran, and by 1231 an army under Chormaqan, sent by the Great Khan Ögedei, had crushed Jalal al-Din Mangburni.

Hülegü, a son of Tolui, a grandson of Genghis Khan and a brother of Möngke and Kublai, was given a fifth of the Mongol army to conquer the Abbasid Caliphate. He destroyed the Nizari Ismaili state in 1256 and the Abbasid Caliphate in 1258, and inherited the West Asian part of the empire after Möngke died in 1259.

Hülegü advanced as far as Gaza and took Aleppo in 1260, but Möngke's death forced him to return to Mongolia for the kuriltai. The small force he left in Palestine was defeated at Ain Jalut by the Mamluks of Egypt. His successor Abaqa beat back an invasion by Berke of the Golden Horde and one by Ghiyas-ud-din Baraq of the Chagatai Khanate. The Mamluks defeated the Mongols at Elbistan in 1277 and again at Homs in 1281.

Under Gaykhatu the realm's finances were ruined, and his vizier's attempt to introduce paper money on the Yuan model largely failed. After Gaykhatu was overthrown in 1295 and his cousin Baydu removed within a year, Ghazan took the throne and was the first ilkhan to convert to Islam. Under Abu Sa'id Bahadur Khan, enthroned in 1316, the realm faced rebellions and invasions. In the 1330s the Black Death ravaged it, and Abu Sa'id, the last ilkhan, died of the plague in 1335. Short-lived khans followed, and in 1357 Jani Beg of the Golden Horde took Tabriz, ending what remained.

Unlike the Yuan dynasty in China, which excluded the native population from high office, the Ilkhanids governed through a Central Asian and Persian administration working with Turco-Mongol military officers. Not every administrator was Muslim or from the old families: the vizier from 1288 to 1291, Sa'ad al-Dawla, was a Jew, and Rashid al-Din Hamadani was a Jewish convert to Islam. Persian bureaucrats promoted the idea of kingship over the Land of Iran, and historians presented the Mongols as heirs of the Sasanian Empire.

The period produced many works of history, the best known being Rashid al-Din's Jami' al-tawarikh, commissioned by Ghazan and presented to Öljeitü in 1307. Hülegü's astronomers built an observatory at Maragheh. Western European courts repeatedly sought an alliance against the Mamluks but never concluded a formal one.
ille-et-vilaine: Ille-et-Vilaine lies in Upper Brittany in the north-west of France and is named after its two main rivers, the Ille and the Vilaine, whose confluence is in Rennes. It is one of the original 83 departments created during the French Revolution on 4 March 1790, formed from part of the province of Brittany. It is bordered by the departments of Manche to the north-east, Mayenne to the east, Maine-et-Loire to the south-east, Loire-Atlantique to the south, Morbihan to the south-west and Côtes-d'Armor to the west and north-west, and by the English Channel to the north. Its boundary with Côtes-d'Armor, 19 metres long, is the shortest of any department of France.

The land is moderately high, with many hills. A dense network of tributaries drains the large basin of Rennes, whose rich farmland is ringed by hills with old forests worked for timber. The Rance forms part of the north-western border and flows into the Channel along the Côte d'Émeraude between Dinard and Saint-Malo. The Couesnon marks the eastern end of the coast, in the flat Bay of Mont Saint-Michel. In the south the Vilaine near Redon has often flooded, partly because the farmland round Rennes was drained too intensively, and some fields there are now left to flood while works regulate the water.

Rennes is the prefecture of the department and the capital of the region of Brittany, and the subprefectures are Fougères, Redon and Saint-Malo. Gallo, a historic minority language of eastern Brittany, is spoken here. Breton was little spoken in this part of Brittany and disappeared for many centuries, but it is taught again today, and both languages are studied at the University of Rennes. The population has grown steadily since the 1960s.
illinois: Illinois lies in the Midwest and is one of the eight states of the Great Lakes region. Most of its western border with Missouri and Iowa is the Mississippi River, the Wabash River forms part of the eastern border with Indiana, the Ohio River marks the southern border with Kentucky, and the northeast reaches into Lake Michigan. The state lies entirely in the Interior Plains, with a small unglaciated area, the Driftless Area, in the extreme north-west, where Charles Mound, at 376 metres, is the highest natural point. The Illinois River bisects the state from north-east to south-west.

The name is the modern spelling of what early French missionaries and explorers called the Illinois Native Americans. It derives from the Miami-Illinois verb irenwe·wa, 'he speaks the regular way', which passed into Ojibwe and then French. The older explanation that it means 'men' is not supported by the Illinois language, and the spelling Illinois began to appear in the early 1670s.

American Indians of successive cultures lived along the waterways for thousands of years; the Koster Site shows 7,000 years of continuous habitation. Cahokia, the largest chiefdom and urban centre of the pre-Columbian Mississippian culture, stood near present-day Collinsville. It had more than 100 platform and burial mounds, a large plaza and a woodhenge of sacred cedar, and its Monks Mound, 30 metres high, is the largest pre-Columbian structure north of the Valley of Mexico.

The French were the first Europeans to arrive, settling near the Mississippi and Illinois rivers in the 17th-century Illinois Country of New France. After American independence in 1783 made the Mississippi the national boundary, settlers arrived from Kentucky by the Ohio River. Illinois became part of the Northwest Territory and achieved statehood in 1818. John Deere's self-scouring steel plow turned the prairie into productive farmland. In the mid-19th century the Illinois and Michigan Canal and a large railroad network made the state a transportation hub, and Chicago became the world's fastest-growing city by the late 19th century. By 1900 industrial and coal-mining jobs had attracted immigrants from Eastern and Southern Europe, and the Great Migration from the South established a large black community.

Springfield is the capital and Chicago the largest city, and the Chicago metropolitan area holds about three-quarters of the state's 12.8 million residents. Two World Heritage Sites lie in Illinois: the Cahokia Mounds and part of the Wright architecture site. Illinois honours Abraham Lincoln with its slogan Land of Lincoln, and the Abraham Lincoln Presidential Library and Museum is in Springfield.
illyria: Illyria was a region in the western part of the Balkan Peninsula, named for the Illyrians, a group of Indo-European speaking peoples who inhabited it. The Greeks first used Illyris for roughly northern and central present-day Albania, down to the valley of the Aoös, the modern Vjosa, and the Bay of Vlorë, neighbouring Macedonia and Epirus. In Roman times Illyria, Illyris and Illyricum came to mean a broader region reaching from the south-eastern Adriatic coast, modern Albania and Montenegro, and its hinterland to the whole eastern Adriatic and the Danube.

The earliest recorded Illyrian kingdom was that of the Enchele in the 8th century BCE, and the era of other kingdoms runs from about 400 BCE. The Autariatae under Pleurias, in 337 BCE, are counted as one. The most notable were those of Bardyllis of the Dardani and of Agron of the Ardiaei, who created the last and best-known Illyrian kingdom. The kingdoms were small and covered only parts of Illyria. Polybius describes peasant infantry fighting under aristocrats, each holding a town, and the monarchy passed by descent, with marriages used as alliances. In the south the kingdoms imitated their Greek neighbours.

Rome defeated Queen Teuta in the First Illyrian War. She withdrew to the Bay of Kotor, and in 228 BCE Rome imposed a protectorate on Issa and Corcyra and on Epidamnos, Apollonia and Oricum. Macedon tried without success to take the southern Illyrian ports as bases for an attack upon the Italian Peninsula. In 168 BCE the Romans defeated Gentius, the last king, at Scodra, and took him to Rome in 165 BCE. Four client republics were set up, and the region was later governed directly as a province with Scodra as its capital.

The Roman province of Illyricum stretched from the river Drilon in Albania to Istria and the river Sava, with its capital at Salona, near modern Split. After a revolt of Pannonians and Daesitiates the province was divided in 10 CE between Pannonia in the north and Dalmatia in the south, but the name Illyria stayed in use in Late Latin and through the medieval period. In the Late Roman Empire it named a praetorian prefecture.

Church history kept the name too. The bishops of Thessalonica appointed papal vicars for Illyricum, and in 515 forty Illyrian bishops renewed their loyalty to Rome under Pope Hormisdas; in the 8th century the patriarchs of Constantinople brought Illyria under their jurisdiction. Jewish communities are attested at Salona, Narona and Sirmium, known from menorahs and inscriptions.
imam-shamil: Shamil was born on 26 June 1797 into an Avar Muslim family in the small village of Gimry, in present-day Dagestan. He was first named Ali, but after an illness his name was changed to Shamuyil, which is pronounced Shamil in the Caucasus. His father, Dengau, was a landlord, and this let Shamil and his friend Ghazi Muhammad study Arabic and logic. He grew up while the Russian Empire expanded into Ottoman and Qajar lands, and many Caucasian peoples united in resistance in what became known as the Caucasian War, which lasted from 1817 to 1864. Shamil became the disciple and counsellor of Ghazi Mollah, the earlier leader of the resistance.

Ghazi Mollah died at the battle of Gimry in 1832, and Shamil was one of only two murids to escape, badly wounded by a bayonet. He rejoined the murids under the second Imam, Hamzat Bek, and when Hamzat Bek was killed in 1834 he became the leader of the resistance. In 1839 he and about 4,000 followers, men, women and children, were besieged by General Pavel Grabbe in the stronghold of Akhoulgo. He refused Grabbe's demand to surrender and accept exile. The Russians stormed the stronghold; Shamil escaped on the first night, and many Dagestani and Chechen chieftains declared loyalty to the Tsar. He then fled to Chechnya and extended his influence over the clans there.

He united quarrelsome peoples through charisma, piety and fairness in applying sharia law, and used guerrilla tactics against the larger Russian army. In 1845 his forces surrounded and destroyed a column of 8,000 to 10,000 men under Count Mikhail Vorontsov in the forests of Chechnya. Shamil hoped for help from Britain, France or the Ottoman Empire, which never came. After the Crimean War Russia redoubled its efforts, and in September 1859 Shamil surrendered.

Shamil was sent to meet Tsar Alexander II and was then exiled to Kaluga. In December 1868 he was allowed to move to Kyiv, where he was given a mansion. In 1869 he received permission to make the Hajj. Sultan Abdulaziz received him at Istanbul, and at Mecca he met Emir Abdelkader. He died in Medina in 1871 and was buried in the Jannatul Baqi.

Peoples of the Northern Caucasus regard him as a hero. Russians came to respect him despite the bloody conquest of Chechnya and Dagestan, and Alexander II is said to have admired his resistance. His grandson Said Shamil was one of the founders of the Mountainous Republic of the Northern Caucasus, set up in 1917 and conquered by Soviet Russia in 1920.
imhotep: Imhotep, whose name means the one who comes in peace, was chancellor to King Djoser, a possible architect of his step pyramid and high priest of the sun god Ra at Heliopolis. Little is known of him as a historical figure. Two contemporary inscriptions on the base of one of Djoser's statues establish him as chancellor, and a graffito on the enclosure wall of Sekhemkhet's unfinished step pyramid suggests that he outlived Djoser by a few years and worked on that king's pyramid, which was abandoned because Sekhemkhet reigned briefly.

He held the unique title bity sensen, literally the King of Lower Egypt, the two brothers, which has been read as meaning he was the king's twin; with no comparable holders the reading remains speculative. If not a relative, he may have been the king's confidant or childhood friend.

Egyptologists, following much later legends, credit Imhotep with the design and building of the Pyramid of Djoser at Saqqara, built during the 3rd Dynasty. He may also have been responsible for the first known use of stone columns to support a building. Stone had appeared sporadically in the Archaic Period, but nothing as large as the step pyramid had been built wholly of stone; earlier kings were buried in mastaba tombs. The ancient Egyptians themselves never credited him as designer of the step pyramid or inventor of stone architecture. Manetho, in the Ptolemaic period, credited him with inventing the method of dressed-stone building under Djoser.

The location of his tomb is unknown. No text from his lifetime mentions skill in medicine or wisdom writing, and none names him for 1,200 years after his death. The first surviving text to name him dates to the time of Amenhotep III and mentions libations poured to him, and his cult in the New Kingdom was distinct from offerings to other commoners. Imhotep is one of fewer than a dozen non-royal Egyptians deified after death, with his cult centred at Memphis.

Healing powers are first attached to him from the Thirtieth Dynasty, about 2,200 years after his death, and the Greeks equated him with Asklepios. The Famine Stela of the Ptolemaic period credits him with ending a seven-year famine under Djoser. A demotic papyrus of the 2nd century CE from Tebtunis tells a long story of him that includes a magical duel with an Assyrian sorceress.
immanuel-kant: Immanuel Kant was born Emanuel on 22 April 1724 in Königsberg, East Prussia, into a Lutheran family. His father, Johann Georg Kant, was a harness-maker from Memel, and his mother was Anna Regina Reuter. He was the fourth of nine children, six of whom reached adulthood. The household stressed Pietist values of religious devotion, humility and a literal reading of the Bible, and his early schooling was strict, with an emphasis on Latin and religious instruction. He changed the spelling of his name to Immanuel after learning Hebrew.

Kant received a licence to lecture at Königsberg in 1755 and taught mathematics, physics, logic and metaphysics. In 1757 he began lecturing on geography, one of the first to teach it as a subject of its own. His Universal Natural History and Theory of the Heavens (1755) set out the nebular hypothesis, in which the Solar System formed from a cloud of gas. He also suggested that other distant nebulae might be other galaxies. In 1756 he published three papers on the 1755 Lisbon earthquake, among the first systematic attempts to explain earthquakes in natural terms. He became a professor in 1770.

The Critique of Pure Reason appeared in 1781, with a heavily revised second edition in 1787. The Critique of Practical Reason followed in 1788 and the Critique of the Power of Judgment in 1790. In 1792 the King's censorship commission opposed the publication of part of his work on religion. He published the book through the University of Jena, which earned him a royal reprimand, and a royal order later required him never to publish or speak publicly about religion. He died in Königsberg on 12 February 1804, saying Es ist gut, 'It is good'.

In the Critique of Pure Reason Kant argues for transcendental idealism: space and time are forms of intuition that structure all experience, and we know only appearances, not things in themselves. He compared this to a Copernican Revolution, proposing that objects of experience conform to the mind's forms of intuition and categories, not the reverse. His aim was to secure both knowledge and morality against scepticism and determinism, and he wrote that he had to deny knowledge in order to make room for faith.
imola: Imola is a city and comune in the Metropolitan City of Bologna, on the river Santerno in the Emilia-Romagna region. It is traditionally considered the western entrance to the historical region of Romagna. Its Roman name was Forum Cornelii, the Forum of Cornelius, after the dictator Sulla, who founded the city around 82 BCE. It was an agricultural and trading centre, notable for its ceramics. The name Imola was first used in the 7th century by the Lombards, who applied it to the fortress now known as the Castellaccio.

According to Paul the Deacon, Imola was in 412 the scene of the marriage of Ataulf, king of the Visigoths, to Galla Placidia, daughter of the emperor Theodosius the Great. With the exarchate of Ravenna it passed under papal authority. In the 10th century and after, it saw incessant wars against Ravenna, Faenza and Bologna, and out of these conflicts came the city's republican constitution. In the contest between pope and emperor it was generally Ghibelline. Pope Benedict XII made Lippo II Alidosi pontifical vicar, and his family held power until 1424, when the condottiero Angelo della Pergola gained the upper hand.

In 1426 the city was restored to the Holy See, and it was conferred on the Sforza, dukes of Milan, in 1434, 1438 and 1470. It was later bestowed as a dowry on Caterina Sforza, bride of Girolamo Riario, nephew of Pope Sixtus IV, and under the Riarii it was embellished with palaces and works of art. Pope Alexander VI deprived Girolamo's son Ottaviano of power, and on 25 November 1499 the city surrendered to Cesare Borgia. In 1504 Imola submitted to Pope Julius II. It remained papal, apart from the years after 1797, until it joined the Kingdom of Sardinia in 1860.

Imola is best known for the Autodromo Enzo e Dino Ferrari, opened in the 1950s. Among its older buildings are the Rocca Sforzesca, built under Girolamo Riario and Caterina Sforza, the cathedral dedicated to San Cassiano, erected between 1187 and 1271, and Palazzo Tozzoni, built between 1726 and 1738 and since 1981 a civic art museum.
imphal: Imphal lies in the Imphal Valley in the extreme east of India, surrounded by nine ranges of hills, at an average elevation of 786 metres. Its climate is humid subtropical, with cool, dry winters and a slightly hot monsoon season. The name comes from two Meitei words, yum, meaning house, and phāl, meaning plenty or beautiful.

Tradition holds that King Pakhangba established Kangla Fort, once the capital of Manipur, in 33 CE. The kingdom had earlier been ruled by kings of the Khaba clan; the Ningthouja dynasty began to rule after the ascension of Nongda Lairen Pakhangba and came to dominate the region in politics and war. Kangla Palace was built by King Khagemba and his son Khunjaoba. In the reign of Maharaja Bhagyachandra there were a number of Burmese invasions, and the kingdom survived with the help of Maharaj Gambhir Singh.

Imphal remained peaceful until 1891, when disputes within the royal family led the British to send J. W. Quinton, and an order to arrest the prince Senapati Tikendrajit angered the people. The resulting Anglo-Manipur War was won by the British. The king, Maharaja Kulachandra, was sentenced to imprisonment and sent to the Cellular Jail in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, and Tikendrajit and Thangal General were hanged. The British destroyed Kangla Palace in the war. The region merged with India in 1949.
The Battle of Imphal was fought between March and July 1944. The Japanese had invaded in order to destroy the Allied forces and then invade India, but were defeated and forced to retreat.

Imphal is the capital of the Indian state of Manipur, with a population of 277,196 at the 2011 census; most people speak Manipuri. Hinduism is the majority religion and Sanamahism the second largest, and the Pakhangba temple stands within Kangla Fort, whose ruins are surrounded by a moat. The Ima Keithel, or Mothers' Market, was established in the 16th century and is run by women vendors. The Imphal War Cemetery commemorates Indian and British soldiers who died in 1944.
imre-nagy: Imre Nagy was born on 7 June 1896 in Kaposvár, in the Kingdom of Hungary, to a family of peasant origin. His father was a carriage driver and later an unskilled worker. After a poor record at the gymnasium he trained as a locksmith and metal fitter.

Conscripted into the Austro-Hungarian Army in 1914, he was wounded on the Italian Front and again on the Eastern Front, where Russian forces took him prisoner in July 1916. In Siberia he joined a Marxist discussion group, and in 1918 he joined the Communist Party of the Foreign Workers of Siberia and fought in the Red Army in the Russian Civil War. He joined the Russian Communist Party in 1920.

Sent by the Hungarian Communist Party to Hungary in 1921, Nagy worked on underground networks and was arrested several times. From 1930 he lived in the Soviet Union, where he did agricultural research and, from 1933 to 1941, served the NKVD as an informer under the codename Volodia.

After the Second World War he returned to Hungary and was Minister of Agriculture, distributing land to the peasants, then Interior Minister. As prime minister from 1953 to 1955 he promoted his New Course, easing the harshest parts of Mátyás Rákosi's Stalinist regime, but Rákosi's influence prevailed and he was dismissed on 18 April 1955, losing his party posts.

After Nikita Khrushchev's Secret Speech of February 1956, criticism of Rákosi grew, and he was forced out in July. On 23 October a student demonstration in Budapest called for Nagy's return, and the revolt began. Nagy was named prime minister on 24 October. On 28 October he negotiated a ceasefire with Soviet representatives and announced the dissolution of the ÁVH secret police.

By 30 October he promised a multi-party system, and on 1 November he announced Hungary's withdrawal from the Warsaw Pact and appealed to the UN for recognition of its neutrality. Soviet forces attacked Budapest on 4 November, and Nagy took refuge in the Yugoslav Embassy.

Despite János Kádár's written safe conduct, he was arrested on 22 November as he left the embassy and taken to Romania. He was secretly tried in Hungary for treason and the organisation of the overthrow of the republic, and hanged on 16 June 1958; his burial was in an unmarked grave in the prison yard. In June 1989 he and other figures of the revolution were rehabilitated and reburied with full honours, an event that played a key part in the fall of the Hungarian Socialist Workers' Party regime.
incandescent-light-bulb: In 1761 Ebenezer Kinnersley demonstrated heating a wire to incandescence, but such wires melted or oxidised very quickly in air. The British physicist and chemist Joseph Swan began working with carbonised paper filaments in an evacuated glass bulb in 1850, and by 1860 he could show a working device. Without a good vacuum and an adequate supply of electricity, however, the bulb lasted only a short time and gave an inefficient light. By the mid-1870s better pumps had become available, and Swan returned to his experiments.

The bulb is an airtight glass envelope, either evacuated or filled with an inert gas, around a filament through which current is passed. The first commercially successful filaments were made from carbonised paper or bamboo. Carbon tended to sublimate and blacken the glass, and its resistance falls as it heats, which made lamps sensitive to the power supply. Modern bulbs use tungsten wire, usually a coiled coil, which runs hotter and evaporates more slowly. A bulb's life is a trade-off between efficiency and longevity: general lamps are set for 1,000 to 2,000 hours, while theatre and projection lamps may last only a few hours.

Historians Robert Friedel and Paul Israel conclude that Edison's version was the first practical implementation because of four factors: an effective filament material, a higher vacuum, a high resistance that made distribution from a central source economically viable, and the development of the components of a large-scale lighting system. Swan's bulb was nonetheless in daily use in London in 1881. Thomas Hughes attributes Edison's business success to his integrated system of electric lighting.

Early bulbs were blown by hand by teams of three workers, and Corning Glass Works made about 150 an hour in the 1880s. Libbey's Westlake machine went into production in 1910, and Corning's Ribbon Machine, installed in 1926, was making 1,000 bulbs per minute by 1939. Less than 5 per cent of the energy a bulb uses becomes visible light, the rest being released as heat.
incense: The word incense comes from the Latin incendere, to burn. The earliest documented use is associated with ancient Nubia: excavations at Qustul in Lower Nubia, in present-day Sudan, found one of the earliest known incense burners, of ceramic, dating to the A-Group culture of about 3300 to 3000 BCE, before Egypt's Early Dynastic period. Its decoration, including processional imagery read by some scholars as royal, suggests that incense already had ritual and political meaning.

In ancient Egypt it was burned to mask unpleasant odours, repel malevolent spirits and honour the gods, and resin balls in prehistoric tombs at El Mahasna show its early place in funerary practice. Reliefs at Deir el-Bahari depict expeditions to obtain incense and aromatic resins. The Babylonians used it in prayers and offerings to oracles, and its use passed from Mesopotamia to Greece and Rome.

Incense is aromatic plant material that releases fragrant smoke when burnt, made from local ingredients: sage and cedar among the indigenous peoples of North America, agarwood and sandalwood in China and Japan. It comes in two main kinds. Indirect-burning incense, such as the resins frankincense and myrrh, needs a separate heat source such as charcoal.

Direct-burning incense is a paste of ground fragrant material and an odourless binder, shaped into sticks, coils or cones, which smoulders once lit. Coils burn for hours or days and are common in Chinese cultures, while cones were invented in Japan in the 1800s. Trade in incense materials formed a major part of commerce along the Silk Road and the Incense Route.

Incense has served practical, aesthetic and religious ends. Its strong scent covered the smell of decay in funerals. It is offered to deities in Jewish, Christian, Taoist and Buddhist worship, and many cultures have seen the rising smoke as prayer directed to a deity on high. The incense of the Jewish Temple in Jerusalem, called ketoret, is stated in the Book of Exodus to be a mixture of stacte, onycha, galbanum and frankincense.

In China, calibrated incense sticks and incense clocks came with Buddhism, and the poet Yu Jianwu (487–551) wrote of telling the night's hours by burning incense. In Japan the art of incense appreciation is called kōdō, and in many Arab countries scented chips called bakhoor are burned to welcome guests.
incheon: Incheon has been inhabited since the Neolithic. The first historical record of the area dates from 475 CE, in the reign of King Jangsu of Goguryeo, under the name Michuhol, which is supposed to have stood on the modern Munhak Hill. The area changed names with successive kingdoms. In the Goryeo era it was called Gyeongwon or Inju, and the present name dates from 1413. Old Incheon had its centre at Gwangyo-dong, where the prefecture office and the local academy stood.

Only 4,700 people lived there when it became an international port in 1883. The other historical name, Jemulpo or Chemulpo, came into wide use only with the opening of the port, and the city centre moved from Gwangyo to Jemulpo. During Japanese rule it was internationally known as Jinsen, from the Japanese pronunciation of its Sino-Korean name. In 1914 the Japanese colonial government merged its outer parts with Bupyeong County to form Bucheon County, and between 1936 and 1940 part of that county was recombined into Incheon. The first shots of the Russo-Japanese War were fired at the Battle of Chemulpo Bay.

North Korean troops occupied Incheon on 4 July 1950. In the Battle of Inchon UN troops landed to relieve pressure on the Pusan Perimeter and to launch an offensive northward, a decisive UN victory, and the city was recaptured on 19 September 1950. The USS Inchon was named after it. Incheon was separated from Gyeonggi Province as a Directly Governed (now Metropolitan) City on 1 July 1981, and neighbouring islands and parts of Gimpo County and Ganghwa were added in 1989 and 1995. It was spelled Inchon until South Korea adopted a new Romanization system in 2000. Pro-democracy protests took place there before and during the June Democratic Movement of 1987.

Incheon is a city in north-western South Korea, bordering Seoul and Gyeonggi Province to the east, and part of the Seoul Metropolitan Area. About 3 million people live there. It is a major transportation hub in northeast Asia, with Incheon International Airport and Incheon Port. In 2003 it was designated South Korea's first free economic zone, and it hosted the Asian Games in 2014.
india: Modern humans reached the Indian subcontinent from Africa by about 55,000 years ago. Neolithic and chalcolithic cultures arose around Mehrgarh after 7000 BCE and gradually evolved into the Indus Valley Civilisation, which flourished during 2500 to 1900 BCE around cities such as Mohenjo-daro, Harappa and Dholavira. Between 1500 and 1200 BCE an archaic form of Sanskrit diffused into India from the northwest, and its evidence is found in the Rig Veda. By the middle of the first millennium BCE caste, or varna, had emerged in the cities of the central Ganges plain, and Jainism and Buddhism arose, both stressing non-violence and rejecting birth into a fixed hereditary varna.

The Maurya Empire followed, and under Ashoka (ca. 268 to 232 BCE) it briefly controlled the major urban hubs of the subcontinent, except in the deep south. Early in the 2nd millennium Muslim armies from Central Asia intermittently overran the northern plains, eventually establishing the Delhi Sultanate. Sikhism emerged in the Punjab, and the Mughal Empire brought two centuries of economic expansion and relative peace. The British East India Company consolidated territorial control, and crown rule, the British Raj, began in 1858. A nationalist movement, noted for nonviolent resistance after 1920, was a major factor in ending British rule. In 1947 the British Indian Empire was partitioned into the dominions of India and Pakistan, a partition that brought large-scale loss of life and unprecedented migration.

The Constitution of India, drafted between 1946 and 1949, took effect on 26 January 1950 and made India a federal republic with a democratic parliamentary system. It makes untouchability illegal. The Lok Sabha, the lower house, has 543 elected members. The reorganisation of states in 1956 followed linguistic lines. India's population was 361 million in 1951. Economic reforms of the 1990s reopened the economy to the world. India has 45 UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
indian-national-congress: During the later 1870s Indians made concerted efforts to found a pan-Indian organisation with nationalist political influence. In 1883 Allan Octavian Hume, a retired British civil servant known for his pro-Indian activities, set out the idea of a body representing Indian interests in an open letter to graduates of the University of Calcutta. Its aim was to win a greater share in government for educated Indians. A meeting planned for Poona was moved to Bombay because of a cholera outbreak, and the first session of the Congress was held there from 28 to 31 December 1885. Hume organised it with the approval of the Viceroy, Lord Dufferin, and served as general secretary.

From its start the Congress was led by Moderates influenced by Western liberalism, who demanded the rule of law and equality regardless of caste, creed or sex. By 1905 it had divided in two. The Moderates, among them Dadabhai Naoroji and Gopal Krishna Gokhale, sought self-government by peaceful, constitutional means within the British Empire. The Extremists, led by Lala Lajpat Rai, Bipin Chandra Pal and Bal Gangadhar Tilak, favoured a more confrontational course.

Mahatma Gandhi returned from South Africa in 1915 and joined the Congress. After the First World War the party came to be associated with him as its unofficial spiritual leader. In 1920 he allied with the Khilafat Movement against British rule, using civil disobedience, or satyagraha, as his tool, and in 1922 he suspended the agitation after policemen were killed at Chauri Chaura.

After independence in 1947 the Congress dominated Indian politics. In the first general election of 1952 it won 364 of 479 contested seats, and it held power nationally until 1977. Its first prime minister, Jawaharlal Nehru, led it to support a mixed economy, the Planning Commission and Five-Year Plans. In 1969 the party split, and from 1975 to 1977 Indira Gandhi declared a state of emergency.

The party has governed India for more than 54 years, with six prime ministers from its ranks, the first being Nehru. Under Nehru it oversaw the founding of institutions such as the Indian Institutes of Technology and the All India Institute of Medical Sciences, and it helped shape India's non-aligned foreign policy during the Cold War.
indian-ocean: The Indian Ocean covers 70,560,000 km2, about 20% of the water area of the Earth's surface, with an average depth of 3,741 m. It is bounded by Asia to the north, Africa to the west and Australia to the east, and to the south by the Southern Ocean or Antarctica, depending on the definition in use. Its large marginal seas include the Andaman Sea, the Arabian Sea, the Bay of Bengal and the Laccadive Sea. In 1953 the International Hydrographic Organization drew its borders to include the Southern Ocean; in 2002 it delimited the Southern Ocean separately.

Unlike the Atlantic and Pacific, the Indian Ocean is enclosed by major landmasses on three sides and does not stretch from pole to pole. Its climate is governed by the monsoon, the strongest on Earth. Strong north-east winds blow from October until April, and from May until October south and west winds prevail. The monsoon reverses the large seasonal currents, including the Somali Current.

The Indian Ocean, together with the Mediterranean, has connected people since ancient times, whereas the Atlantic and Pacific long acted as barriers. The ocean is named after India, which projects into it, and has been known by its present name since at least 1515, when the Latin form Oceanus Orientalis Indicus is attested. Ancient Greek geography called the part known to the Greeks the Erythraean Sea. Chinese explorers of the 15th century, such as Zheng He of the Ming dynasty, called it the Western Oceans.

The written history of the ocean has been largely Eurocentric, because it depends on the sources of the European colonial era. It is often divided into an ancient period and an Islamic period, followed by Portuguese, Dutch, French and British periods. A concept of an Indian Ocean World, based on the monsoon that linked Asia, China, India and Mesopotamia, is sometimes called the first global economy. It developed independently of European trade in the Mediterranean and Atlantic and remained largely independent of it until the colonial dominance of the 19th century. The first human settlement around its shores dates to the Pleistocene, with fossils of Homo erectus found in India.
indian-rebellion-of-1857: The East India Company had been in India since 1612, but its victory at the Battle of Plassey in 1757 began its firm foothold in eastern India. In 1764 it defeated the Mughal emperor Shah Alam II at the Battle of Buxar and gained the right to collect revenue in Bengal, and the Anglo-Mysore and Anglo-Maratha Wars brought more territory under its control.

The rising had no single cause. Resentment grew over invasive British-style social reforms, harsh land taxes, the summary treatment of some landowners and princes, and doubts about British claims of material improvement. The Bengal Army, which recruited heavily among high-status Hindus and comparatively wealthy Muslims, was the largest of the Company's three armies. The immediate flashpoint is often linked to the Pattern 1853 Enfield rifle-musket, whose greased paper cartridges were opened with the teeth. In early 1857 a rumour spread that the grease was cow tallow, offensive to Hindus, and pig lard, offensive to Muslims.

The rebellion began on 10 May 1857 with a mutiny of sepoys at Meerut, 40 miles northeast of Delhi. Early on 11 May the 3rd Cavalry reached Delhi and called on the 81-year-old Mughal ruler Bahadur Shah II to lead them, and he was proclaimed Emperor. Most accounts hold that he was coerced. His adhesion turned the Sikhs of the Punjab away from the rebellion, and the large princely states, including Hyderabad, Mysore, Travancore and Kashmir, did not join it.

Rebels took large parts of the North-Western Provinces and Awadh. At Lucknow, Sir Henry Lawrence fortified the Residency, and after 90 days of siege the defenders were reduced to 300 loyal sepoys, 350 British soldiers and 550 non-combatants. Rani Lakshmi Bai of Jhansi, whose state had been annexed under the doctrine of lapse, became a centre of revolt. British forces retook Kanpur by mid-July and Delhi by the end of September 1857, and the rebels were defeated at Gwalior on 20 June 1858.

Both sides committed atrocities against civilians. Rebels killed British officers and civilians, including women and children, and British reprisals fell on rebels and their supporters, sometimes entire villages. Some estimates put the toll in Awadh alone at 150,000 Indians killed, 100,000 of them civilians. Bahadur Shah II was tried for treason and exiled to Rangoon, where he died in 1862, ending the Mughal dynasty.

The Government of India Act 1858 dissolved the East India Company and placed India under the Crown. The Bengal Army was scaled back and recruitment in the Punjab increased. The name remains contested: Indian Mutiny, Revolt of 1857 and First War of Independence are all used.
indira-gandhi: Indira Nehru was born on 19 November 1917 in Allahabad, into a Kashmiri Pandit family. Her father, Jawaharlal Nehru, was a leading figure in the movement for independence from British rule. She was her parents' only surviving child and grew up with her mother, Kamala Nehru, at the Anand Bhavan estate. Her childhood was lonely: her father was often away or in prison, and her mother, frequently ill, died of tuberculosis in February 1936. She studied in India and Switzerland and at Santiniketan, founded by Rabindranath Tagore, and married Feroze Gandhi, with whom she had two sons, Rajiv and Sanjay.

In 1959, as president of the Indian National Congress, she played a part in the dissolution of the communist-led Kerala government. Lal Bahadur Shastri made her minister of information and broadcasting in 1964, and after his death in January 1966 she defeated Morarji Desai in the party's leadership election. Party bosses and the press at first called her a dumb doll, Goongi goodiya in Hindi. The Congress expelled her in 1969, and her faction, the INC (R), won a landslide in 1971 under the slogan Garibi Hatao (Remove Poverty), an answer to the opposition's Indira Hatao.

In 1969 she nationalised fourteen major commercial banks. In December 1971 India intervened in the war in East Pakistan, where the Pakistani army's repression had sent about ten million refugees across the border; it ended in Indian victory and the independence of Bangladesh. India tested a nuclear device in 1974, and Sikkim joined the Indian Union in 1975. After extending the state of emergency twice, she called elections in 1977 and lost her seat as Congress fell from 350 seats to 153. Congress returned in January 1980, and Sanjay died in a plane crash on 23 June.

In Punjab the preacher Jarnail Singh Bhindranwale, whom Congress had helped to prominence, moved into a guest house near the Golden Temple in 1982 with about 200 armed followers. Indira Gandhi was assassinated on 31 October 1984, while chairing the Non-Aligned Movement. World leaders mourned her, and Margaret Thatcher travelled to New Delhi for the funeral. She had received the Bharat Ratna in 1971, and Henry Kissinger's phrase iron lady became her nickname.
indo-european-languages: The Indo-European family is native to the north of the Indian subcontinent, most of Europe and Greater Iran, with further branches in Armenia and parts of the southern subcontinent. Historically its languages were also spoken in Anatolia and north-western China. Eight branches are still spoken: four by hundreds of millions of native speakers each (Indo-Iranian, Italic, Germanic and Balto-Slavic) and four by fewer than fifteen million each (Hellenic, Albanoid, Armenian and Celtic). Two major branches, Anatolian and Tocharian, are extinct.

Over 3.4 billion people speak an Indo-European language as a first language, the most of any language family. Ethnologue estimates about 446 living languages, of which 313 belong to the Indo-Iranian branch. Several European languages, among them English, French, Portuguese, Russian, Spanish and Dutch, spread through colonialism in the modern period.

All Indo-European languages descend from a single prehistoric language, reconstructed as Proto-Indo-European and spoken sometime in the Neolithic or early Bronze Age. Its homeland is the subject of competing hypotheses. The academic consensus supports the Kurgan hypothesis, which places it on the Pontic–Caspian steppe, in what is now Ukraine and southern Russia, in association with the Yamnaya culture.

The oldest records are isolated Hittite words and names in Assyrian texts from Kültepe in eastern Anatolia, dating to the 20th century BCE. The Anitta text, in Hittite, dated to 1700 BCE, is the oldest known text in an Indo-European language, and fragmentary Mycenaean Greek records date from between 1450 and 1350 BCE. How the parent language split into its branches is not attested, and the timeline is disputed: David Anthony places Pre-Anatolian at about 4200 BCE and Proto-Indo-Iranian at about 2200 BCE.

European visitors to the Indian subcontinent began to notice similarities among Indo-Aryan, Iranian and European languages in the 16th century. In 1583 the Jesuit Thomas Stephens wrote from Goa of likenesses between North Indian languages and Greek and Latin, and in 1585 the merchant Filippo Sassetti compared Sanskrit and Italian words, such as sapta and sette for seven. Neither led to further inquiry. In 1647 the Dutch scholar Marcus Zuerius van Boxhorn proposed a common ancestor that he called Scythian.

In 1786 Sir William Jones told the Asiatic Society of Bengal that Sanskrit, Greek and Latin bore a stronger affinity than could have arisen by accident and had sprung from some common source which perhaps no longer existed. The analysis of these relationships and the reconstruction of their common source were central to the development of historical linguistics as a discipline in the 19th century. The current consensus accepts no genetic link between the family and any other language family.
indonesia: Indonesia is an equatorial archipelago of coastal plains, mountains and volcanic islands, extending 5,120 kilometres from east to west across three time zones and 1,760 kilometres from north to south. Published counts of its islands range from 13,000 to 25,000, and the most widely cited official count is 17,508, with about 6,000 inhabited.

Its five main islands are Sumatra, Java, Sulawesi, Borneo and New Guinea. Strategic shipping routes between the Indian and Pacific oceans run through the Malacca, Sunda and Lombok straits. The country lies on a complex plate-boundary zone, with at least 127 active volcanoes and a high exposure to earthquakes and tsunamis; the Toba super-eruption about 74,000 years ago was one of the largest known.

Java has yielded hominin fossils generally attributed to Homo erectus, and narrative cave art in Sulawesi has been dated to a minimum age of 51,200 years. From the third millennium BCE Austronesian-speaking communities moved south from Taiwan through the Philippines into the archipelago, and from around 500 BCE regional trading networks connected it with South and East Asia.

In the early centuries CE some coastal communities in Borneo, Sumatra and Java developed into trading ports, and Indian merchants and religious specialists brought Sanskrit literacy, Hindu and Buddhist practices and models of kingship that local rulers adopted. Srivijaya, founded in southeastern Sumatra in the late 7th century, became a maritime trading polity and a centre of Buddhist learning.

Rulers in central Java supported the building of Borobudur and Prambanan between the 8th and 10th centuries. Majapahit emerged in eastern Java in the late 13th century after Raden Wijaya used a Mongol expedition to defeat his rivals and then forced the Mongols to withdraw.

Its rulers claimed suzerainty over ports across the archipelago, although beyond Java this authority was often exercised indirectly through tributary, ritual and commercial relationships. Islamic states grew from the late medieval period, and European powers competed to monopolise trade in the Spice Islands of Maluku. Dutch commercial and colonial control expanded from the 17th century and covered most of the archipelago by the early 20th century.

Indonesia proclaimed its independence in the aftermath of World War II. After the fall of Suharto in 1998, decentralisation transferred substantial lawmaking powers to provincial, regency and city governments, and constitutional amendments between 1999 and 2002 introduced direct presidential elections, which began in 2004. The country is a presidential republic of 38 provinces.

The Javanese are the largest ethnic group, at about 40%. More than 700 languages are spoken, and Indonesian, a standardised variety of Malay adopted as a language of unity through the 1928 Youth Pledge, is the official language. Its motto, Bhinneka Tunggal Ika, comes from the 14th-century poem Sutasoma.
indonesia-raya: While living in Jakarta, Wage Rudolf Supratman, a musician and young reporter, read an essay in Timbul magazine that challenged Indonesian music experts to compose a future national anthem. He took up the challenge, and the song, titled Indonesia, was completed in Bandung in 1924. According to Tempo the words were revised after Supratman was reportedly inspired by Tan Malaka's book Massa Actie, published in 1926, and the song went through several revisions before reaching its final form in 1928.

That year youths from across Indonesia held the first Indonesian Youth Congress to push for independence. Supratman asked the organisers for access to report on it, and they asked him not to publish, for fear that the Dutch authorities would ban the event. Encouraged by the leader Sugondo Djojopuspito, he played the song on the violin on 28 October 1928, at the Second Indonesian Youth Congress, hoping it would one day become the national anthem.

After the congress many political and student organisations distributed the text, and the press played a key part. The daily Soeloeh Ra'jat Indonesia published the words on 7 November 1928, and the Chinese Indonesian weekly Sin Po followed on 10 November, an act of defiance towards the Dutch. In 1929 Supratman retitled the song Indonesia Raya, Great Indonesia, and printed pamphlets himself; all one thousand copies sold quickly. The businessman Tio Tek Hong issued the first records that year, but in 1930 the Dutch colonial authorities banned the song and confiscated the unsold records.

The first stanza was chosen as the national anthem when independence was proclaimed on 17 August 1945, and the constitution and a state gazette of 1958 confirm that only that stanza serves as the anthem. It is played at flag-raising ceremonies in schools every Monday, and at the main ceremony on 17 August each year.

The song marked the birth of the archipelago nationalist movement that aimed to end Dutch colonial rule. Because there was no orchestral version, the Indonesian government asked the Dutch arranger Jozef Cleber in 1950 for a symphonic one. President Sukarno found his first recording too frilly and wanted something solemn like the Dutch Wilhelmus. Cleber considered that impossible, saw some of the character of the Marseillaise in the tune, and made a second arrangement marked maestoso con bravura, which Sukarno approved. It remained in use for 47 years, until a remastered version by Addie MS in 1998.

Supratman died in 1938, and his four surviving sisters inherited the rights. The state became owner when the song became the national anthem, and in 1958 the government obtained the sole right from his family, rewarding each sister with 250,000 rupiah in 1960.
indra: Indra is of ancient but unclear origin, and the roots of his name have been contested among scholars since the 19th century. Aspects of him resemble other Indo-European thunder gods, such as Zeus, Thor and Perun, who are linked to rain and thunder and share parts of his heroic mythology. A tablet from Boghaz-köi, dated to about 1400 BCE, records a treaty that names Mitra, Varuna, Indra and Nasatya among its gods. Modern scholarship suggests that the name arose at the Bactria–Margiana Archaeological Complex, where the Aryans lived before settling in India.

More than a quarter of the 1,028 hymns of the Rigveda mention Indra, which makes him the deity referred to most often. The commonest theme is his killing, with his thunderbolt, of the serpent Vritra, which held back the rains; the rivers are thereby released. In the Rigveda he is armed with a thunderbolt, the vajra, rides a chariot and has golden hair. In later art he rides a four-tusked white elephant, Airavata, and the rainbow is called his bow. His abode is Amaravati, the capital of Svarga.

In post-Vedic texts his importance declines and he is shown as an intoxicated, hedonistic god, a minor figure beside Vishnu, Shiva or Devi.
