The Puranas, the Ramayana and the Mahabharata make him a son of the sage Kashyapa and of Aditi, and husband of Shachi. According to the Vishnu Purana, Indra is a title borne by the king of the gods, which changes with each Manvantara, a cyclic period of time in Hindu cosmology.

In Buddhism Indra, called Śakra or Sakka, rules over the Trāyastriṃśa heaven above Mount Sumeru, one of the realms of rebirth, and Buddhist texts reduce him to a figurehead who himself suffers rebirth. In Jainism he is not the king of the gods but the king of superhumans in Svarga-Loka, and Jain literature knows sixty-four Indras who attend the five auspicious events in the life of a Tirthankara. In Iranian religion the roles were reversed, and the Vendidad names Indra as a relatively minor demon. Tamil Sangam literature describes a month-long festival for Indra, the Indra Vila, held for want of rain.
indus: The Indus is 3,180 kilometres long. It rises in the Tibet Autonomous Region of China, where it is known as Sengge Zangbo, flows northwest through Ladakh and Gilgit-Baltistan, and bends sharply to the left after the Nanga Parbat massif. It then runs south-by-southwest through Pakistan and empties into the Arabian Sea near Karachi. Its left-bank tributary on the plains is the Panjnad, formed by the successive confluences of the five Punjab rivers: the Chenab, Jhelum, Ravi, Beas and Sutlej. Its principal right-bank tributaries are the Shyok, Gilgit, Kabul, Kurram and Gomal.

Its headwaters, with those of the Yarlung Tsangpo to the east, follow the suture where the Indian plate collided with the Eurasian plate about 50 million years ago. Its traditional name in Sanskrit and Tibetan is Sindhu, a word for river, and the English name derives through Greek and Old Persian from the same root, as do Hindustan and India.

The cities of the Indus Valley Civilisation, such as Harappa and Mohenjo-daro, date back to around 3300 BCE and were among the largest human settlements of the ancient world. The civilisation reached from northeast Afghanistan to Pakistan and northwest India, and over 1,052 cities and settlements have been found, mainly around the Ghaggar-Hakra River and its tributaries; only about 40 sites lie on the Indus and its tributaries. Its people were the first to build irrigation canals in the valley, and the Kushan and Mughal empires later built canals too.

In the 2nd millennium BCE the Punjab was called Sapta Sindhu in the Rigveda and Hapta Həndu in the Avesta, both meaning seven rivers. Early kingdoms of the valley included Gandhāra and Sindhu-Sauvīra. The river became known to the western world when King Darius of Persia sent his Greek subject Scylax of Caryanda to explore it, about 515 BCE. In 1850 the British East India Company introduced modern irrigation and restored old canals, and the British supervised the building of one of the most complex irrigation networks in the world.

The Indus is the chief supplier of water to the plains of Punjab and Sindh, where rainfall is meagre, and it is the backbone of agriculture in Pakistan. The river is sacred to Hindus, and the Sindhu Darshan Festival is held on its banks at Leh. The Indus River dolphin is found only in this river.
indus-valley-civilisation: The civilisation lasted from 3300 BCE to 1300 BCE, and in its mature form from 2600 BCE to 1900 BCE, across much of Pakistan, north-western India and north-eastern Afghanistan. Its area was larger than ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia combined. It is called Harappan after Harappa, the first site excavated, in the 1920s. The early Harappan cultures grew out of Neolithic cultures, of which the best known is at Mehrgarh in Balochistan, one of the earliest sites of farming and herding in South Asia. A gradual drying of the region during the third millennium BCE may have stimulated urbanisation, and flood-supported farming produced surpluses that supported cities.

Over a thousand Mature Harappan sites have been reported, but there are only five major urban centres: Mohenjo-daro, Harappa, Ganeriwala, Dholavira and Rakhigarhi. Mohenjo-daro and Harappa probably held 30,000 to 60,000 people each. The cities were noted for grid planning, baked-brick houses, covered drains and water supply, and merchants traded by caravan with Central Asia and the Iranian plateau.

Around 1900 BCE signs of decline appeared, and by about 1700 BCE most cities were abandoned. In 1953 Sir Mortimer Wheeler proposed that Aryan invaders caused the end, but scholars rejected this because the skeletons he cited belonged to a later period. Many now point to drought, a weakening monsoon and a decline in trade with Egypt and Mesopotamia. After 1900 BCE the number of sites in India rose from 218 to 853, as people moved east.

Archaeology gives no direct answer about who ruled the cities. The consistency of weights and measures and the uniform planning suggest some central authority, and theories range from a single state to self-governing city states. An ivory scale from Lothal has a smallest division of about 1.704 millimetres. Craftsmen worked copper and bronze alloyed with tin, arsenic and lead. Between 400 and 600 distinct symbols of the undeciphered Indus script are known, and typical inscriptions are about five characters long. Interpretations of Indus religion are largely speculative. Mohenjo-daro was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1980 and Dholavira in 2021.
industrial-revolution: Several factors enabled industrialisation: high agricultural productivity, as in the British Agricultural Revolution, which supplied surplus labour and food; managerial and entrepreneurial skills; ports, rivers, canals and roads that moved raw materials and goods cheaply; natural resources such as coal, iron and waterfalls; political stability and a legal system that supported business; and capital available to invest. Innovations such as Jethro Tull's seed drill of 1701 and Andrew Meikle's threshing machine of 1784 cut the labour that farming required. Before the change, most manufacturing took place in China and India, and India, China and parts of the Middle East produced most of the world's cotton cloth.

The textile industry was the first to use modern production methods. In 1750 Britain imported 2.5 million pounds of raw cotton, mostly spun and woven by hand in Lancashire homes and workshops. By 1787 raw cotton consumption was 22 million pounds, most of it spun on machines, and in 1800 the industry used 52 million pounds. Mechanised spinning powered by water and later steam raised output per worker by a factor of around 500, and the power loom by a factor of 40.

Coke replaced charcoal in iron making: in 1720 Britain made 20,500 tons of charcoal iron and 400 tons with coke, and in 1806 coke cast iron reached 250,000 tons. John Roebuck's lead chamber process of 1746 began large-scale chemical production. Steam supplied an estimated 10,000 horsepower in Britain by 1800 and 210,000 by 1815, though water and wind supplied most industrial power early on. William Murdoch's gas lighting reached London between 1812 and 1820, and steam locomotives came in the early 19th century. Mechanised production spread to continental Europe and the United States by about 1840.

Historians debate the precise start and end of the Industrial Revolution and the pace of its changes. Growth slowed from the late 1830s as markets for the early innovations matured, and revived after 1870 with the steel-making, assembly-line and electrical innovations of the Second Industrial Revolution. The earliest recorded use of the term Industrial Revolution was in 1799, by the French envoy Louis-Guillaume Otto, and Arnold Toynbee's lectures of 1881 are credited with popularising it.

Output and population grew at unprecedented rates. Visible poverty, a growing population and new wealth caused tensions between rich and poor, which led to ideas such as socialism, communism and anarchism. Children as young as eight worked in textile mills. Economists such as Robert Lucas Jr. hold that for the first time the living standards of ordinary people began sustained growth, while others say they did not improve meaningfully until the 20th century. After the Industrial Revolution most manufacturing took place in North America and Western Europe.
ingush-people: The Ingush call themselves Ghalghai, a name most often linked to the word ghāla, tower or fortress, so that it means people of towers. Georgian sources knew them as Gligvi and Dzurdzuks, and Russian sources as Kists. Their ethnonym Ingush comes from the medieval village of Angusht, which by the end of the 17th century was a large settlement in the Tarskoye Valley.

In the early Bronze Age the territory of Ingushetia lay where the Maykop and Kuro-Araxes cultures met, and the Koban culture, dated from the 12th to the 4th century BCE, is usually tied to the origins of the proto-Ingush. Late in the 1st millennium BCE Koban tribes formed a large union known as Malkh or, in Georgian sources, Dzurdzuketi, which controlled the Darial Gorge. It was defeated at the beginning of the 2nd century BCE by the Seleucid king Antiochus III.

From the late 9th to the early 13th century the Ingush belonged to the kingdom of the Alans, and some Ingush researchers place its capital, Magas, on the territory of present-day Ingushetia. On 4 to 6 March 1770, 24 Ingush elders swore an oath of allegiance to the Russian Empire at Barta-Bos, near Angusht, although each side treated such oaths as a union treaty and relations stayed much the same.

In the 19th century the Ingush resisted Russian expansion in the Caucasian War and were considered half-conquered. In 1860 their lands formed the Ingushskiy Okrug of the Terek Oblast, and the 1897 census counted 47,409 Ingush in the empire.

In the Soviet period an Ingush alphabet based on the Latin script was introduced in 1923 and the first newspaper in the language, Serdalo, appeared that year. The 1939 census counted 92,120 Ingush. They were exiled en masse in 1944. In 1992 the Republic of Ingushetia was formed within the Russian Federation, and armed clashes with Ossetians over the Prigorodny district of North Ossetia killed 583 people according to the Russian prosecutor's office. The capital Magas was founded in 1995.

The Ingush are predominantly Sunni Muslims and speak the Ingush language. Their society was traditionally classless, built on clans and unwritten law, with about 350 clans in Ingushetia today. Villages were governed by senior family members and acted together only in great danger, and the Ingush had no titles giving civil authority over others. Their stone architecture is tied to life in the mountains: a family had a tower, a church and a necropolis. Combat towers usually had five or six levels and a stepped pyramidal roof, with the entrance on the second floor.
inn-river: The Inn is a right tributary of the Danube and its third largest by discharge. It rises in the Swiss Alps, west of St. Moritz in the Engadine, a valley named after the river and the only Swiss valley whose waters end in the Black Sea. Soon after its source the river passes through its largest lakes, Lake Sils and Lake Silvaplana. It runs north-eastwards into Austria and from Landeck eastwards through Tyrol and its capital Innsbruck, then crosses into Bavaria near Kufstein. There it passes Rosenheim and Wasserburg am Inn, turns east at Mühldorf, and takes in the Alz and the Salzach. From there to Passau it forms the border between Bavaria and Upper Austria, passing Braunau am Inn and Schärding.

At Passau, where the Ilz also joins, the Inn enters the Danube. Its average flow at the mouth is 735 cubic metres a second, greater than the Danube's at that point, and its watershed holds Piz Bernina, the highest point in the Danube basin. It is still counted as the tributary because the Danube is longer, drains a larger area and flows more evenly.

The name comes from old Celtic words, en and enios, meaning water. The first written mention, in a Roman text of the years 105 to 109, speaks of Sextilius Felix being sent to seize the banks of the Aenus, which flows between the Rhaetian and the Noric peoples. Greek and Latin authors called it Ainos or Aenus, and medieval Latin wrote Enus or Oenus; the Old Bavarian change from e to i turned Enus into In. The double n appeared in the 16th century, as in the Tyrolian Landreim of 1557. The Tyrolean section was first called Aenus by Venantius Fortunatus in the 6th century.
Since at least the 16th century the source has been placed uniformly in the lakes by the Maloja Pass, though it was once believed to lie near the Reschen Pass.

The river is also known for floods. On 3 June 2013 its discharge at Passau reached 6,820 cubic metres a second and its level 12.85 metres, the highest recorded flood level there since 1501, and the old centre of Passau was severely flooded. Today 24 hydroelectric power plants stand on the Inn.
inner-mongolia: Inner Mongolia is a long, narrow region along the north of China. It borders eight provincial-level divisions and shares two-thirds of the length of China's border with the country of Mongolia, as well as a small section with Russia. Because it stretches so far from east to west, its eastern part is often counted with Northeastern China and its western part with North China. The winters are very long, cold and dry, the springs arid with large sandstorms, and the summers warm to hot. The terms Inner and Outer Mongolia in Chinese derive from the Manchu words dorgi and tulergi.

Before the rise of the Mongols in the 13th century, the central and western parts, especially the Hetao region, passed back and forth between Chinese farming communities in the south and northern peoples including the Xiongnu, Xianbei, Khitan, Jurchen and Tujue. The history of the east is mostly one of alternating Tungusic and Mongol tribes. After Genghis Khan unified the Mongol tribes in 1206, the Western Xia was conquered in 1227 and the Jin dynasty fell in 1234. Kublai Khan founded the Yuan dynasty in 1271, and his summer capital Shangdu (Xanadu) stood near present-day Dolonnor.

After the Ming overthrew the Yuan in 1368, they took parts of the region and rebuilt the Great Wall roughly along its present southern edge. After the Tumu incident of 1449, when the Oirat ruler Esen taishi captured the Chinese emperor, Mongols moved south from Outer Mongolia, and until 1635 Inner Mongolia was the political and cultural centre of the Mongols of the Northern Yuan. The Manchus gained far-reaching control of its tribes in 1635, when Ligden Khan's son surrendered the Chakhar Mongols, and the Qing dynasty administered the Mongolian Plateau differently in each region.

Outer Mongolia gained independence from the Qing in 1911, and almost all banners of Inner Mongolia recognised the Bogd Khan as supreme ruler of the Mongols, though internal strife prevented unification. The Republic of China suppressed the Mongol rebellions and reorganised the region into provinces, among them Rehe and Chahar. After the Second World War the Chinese Communists, with Soviet support, established the Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region in 1947. It first covered only the Hulunbuir region and was expanded westwards over the next decade into its present elongated shape under its leader Ulanhu.

The Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region has Hohhot as its capital, with Baotou, Chifeng, Tongliao and Ordos among its other major cities. Han Chinese form the majority of the population, and the region has the largest Mongol population in the world, with over 4 million people. Mongolian is written in the traditional Mongolian script. Herding is the traditional subsistence of the grasslands, and Buddhist temples such as Dazhao, built in 1580, survive in Hohhot.
innsbruck: Innsbruck stands on the River Inn at its junction with the Wipp Valley, which gives access to the Brenner Pass 30 kilometres to the south. It lies in a broad valley between high mountains, the Karwendel Alps to the north and the Patscherkofel and the Serles to the south. The name means bridge over the Inn, and the town began in the Middle Ages as a strategic crossing of the river.

In the 4th century the Romans set up an army station, Veldidena, at Oenipons, as Innsbruck was then called, to guard the commercial road from Verona over the Brenner to Augsburg in their province of Raetia. The name Veldidena survives in the district of Wilten. In 1363 Innsbruck came under Habsburg control, and in 1429 it became the capital of all Tyrol.

In the 1490s Emperor Maximilian I also resided in the city, and it became a centre of European politics and culture. A regular postal service between Innsbruck and Mechelen was set up in 1490. The Golden Roof was completed around 1500, and the Court Church holds a funeral monument for Maximilian, partly erected by his successors, with a cenotaph and bronze statues of real and mythical ancestors of the emperor. After the Treaty of Pressburg the city was for a time part of Bavaria, and it returned to Austria after the Congress of Vienna.
Austria was annexed by Nazi Germany in 1938. Innsbruck held two subcamps of the Dachau concentration camp, and between 1943 and April 1945 it suffered twenty-two air raids and heavy damage.

Innsbruck is the capital of the Austrian state of Tyrol and the fifth-largest city in Austria, with 132,188 inhabitants. It hosted the Winter Olympics in 1964 and 1976 and the Winter Paralympics in 1984 and 1988. Among its modern buildings is the Bergisel ski jump, designed by Zaha Hadid and completed in 2002.
insulin: In 1869 Paul Langerhans, a medical student in Berlin, noticed clumps of tissue scattered through the pancreas, later called the islets of Langerhans. In 1889 Oskar Minkowski and Joseph von Mering removed the pancreas from a healthy dog and found sugar in its urine, establishing for the first time a link between the pancreas and diabetes. In 1901 Eugene Lindsay Opie showed that the disease arose from destruction of the islets.

In October 1920 Frederick Banting concluded that digestive secretions were breaking down the islet secretion and making extraction impossible. As a surgeon he knew that blocking the pancreatic duct would make most of the pancreas atrophy while leaving the islets intact, and he reasoned that a relatively pure extract could then be made. He and Charles Best, working in John Macleod's laboratory at the University of Toronto, were the first to isolate insulin from dog pancreas in 1921.

Insulin is a peptide hormone made by the beta cells of the pancreatic islets, and its name comes from the Latin for island. It regulates the metabolism of carbohydrates, fats and protein by promoting the absorption of glucose from the blood into the liver, fat and skeletal muscle. Decreased or absent insulin activity results in diabetes. In type 1 diabetes an autoimmune reaction destroys the beta cells, and in type 2 the tissues become resistant to insulin. Human insulin has 51 amino acids, arranged in an A-chain and a B-chain joined by disulfide bonds.

Tensions arose among the four co-discoverers in January 1922, and James Collip briefly threatened to patent his purification process separately. John G. FitzGerald, director of Connaught Laboratories, made an agreement on 25 January 1922 that none of them would patent the work with a commercial pharmaceutical firm. The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine of 1923 went to Banting and Macleod. Banting, incensed that Best was not mentioned, shared his prize with him, and Macleod shared his with Collip. The patent was sold to the University of Toronto for one dollar.

Insulin was the first peptide hormone discovered. Frederick Sanger determined its amino acid structure in 1951, making it the first protein fully sequenced, and Dorothy Hodgkin determined its three-dimensional structure in 1969. Sanger won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1958 and Rosalyn Sussman Yalow the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1977, for work on insulin.
integrated-circuit: A precursor of the integrated circuit was the micromodule, a small ceramic substrate holding a single miniaturised component, which could be assembled with others into a compact grid. Jack Kilby proposed the idea to the United States Army in 1957, which led to the short-lived Micromodule Program. As that project gained traction, Kilby devised a fundamentally new approach. Newly employed by Texas Instruments, he recorded his first ideas in July 1958, and in his patent application of 6 February 1959 he described a body of semiconductor material in which all the components of the circuit are completely integrated. The first customer was the United States Air Force. Kilby won the 2000 Nobel Prize in physics for his part in the invention.

In its strict sense the term means a monolithic circuit built on a single piece of silicon, though it is also applied to hybrid and multi-chip constructions. Chips are made by a planar process of photolithography, deposition and etching, and printed as a unit rather than built one transistor at a time. This makes them small, cheap and fast, but designing a complex chip costs many tens of millions of dollars and the factories are enormously expensive, so chips pay only where production volumes are high.

Most modern ones rest on the metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistor, developed at Bell Labs between 1955 and 1960. Fred Heiman and Steven Hofstein built the earliest experimental MOS chip, with 16 transistors, at RCA in 1962, and General Microelectronics introduced the first commercial MOS circuit in 1964.

Aerospace projects helped inspire the technology. The Minuteman missile and the Apollo programme both needed lightweight digital computers for inertial guidance. The Apollo Guidance Computer motivated the technology, but it was the Minuteman missile that forced it into mass production. Minuteman and other United States Navy programmes accounted for the whole 4 million dollar integrated circuit market in 1962, and in 1968 government spending on space and defence still made up 37 per cent of a 312 million dollar market.

Complexity then rose by stages, from hundreds of transistors per chip in the late 1960s to tens of thousands by the mid-1970s. One-megabit memory chips, with over a million transistors, appeared in 1986, and microprocessors passed the million mark in 1989 and the billion mark in 2005.
internal-combustion-engine: Various scientists and engineers contributed to the engine's development. In 1791 John Barber developed a gas turbine, and Robert Street's patent of 1794 described an engine that was also the first to use liquid fuel. In 1798 John Stevens built the first American internal combustion engine. In 1807 the Swiss engineer François Isaac de Rivaz invented a hydrogen-based engine ignited by an electric spark, and in 1808 he fitted it to a primitive working vehicle. In 1823 Samuel Brown patented the first internal combustion engine applied industrially. The first such engines did not compress the mixture, and these attempts to imitate the steam engine were very inefficient.

An internal combustion engine burns fuel with an oxidiser, usually air, in a combustion chamber that is part of the engine's working fluid flow circuit, and the expanding gases act directly on parts of the engine. The term usually means engines with intermittent combustion, such as the two-stroke and four-stroke piston engines and the Wankel rotary engine. A second class uses continuous combustion: gas turbines, jet engines and most rocket engines. In external combustion engines, such as steam engines, the working fluid is kept separate from the combustion products. Engines are usually run on hydrocarbon fuels such as gasoline, diesel fuel or natural gas, and as early as 1900 Rudolf Diesel was using peanut oil.

Most internal combustion engines serve in mobile applications and are the primary power supply of cars, aircraft and boats. Reciprocating piston engines are by far the most common power source for land and water vehicles, including automobiles, motorcycles, ships and, to a lesser extent, locomotives. The first engines were started by turning the flywheel, and the Daimler Reitwagen was started with a hand crank. All automobiles with such engines were started this way until Charles Kettering developed the electric starter.
international-committee-of-the-red-cross: Until the middle of the 19th century armies had no organised nursing systems for their casualties and no safe institutions in which to treat the wounded. In June 1859 the Swiss businessman Henry Dunant reached Solferino on the evening of 24 June and saw the aftermath of the Battle of Solferino, in which about 40,000 soldiers died or were left wounded in a single day. Shocked by the suffering and the near-total lack of medical care, he spent several days helping to treat the wounded, organising local people to give aid without discrimination.

Back in Geneva he wrote A Memory of Solferino, published at his own expense in 1862 and sent to leading figures across Europe. It called for national voluntary relief organisations to nurse wounded soldiers and for international treaties guaranteeing the neutrality and protection of the wounded and of medics. The first Geneva Convention was signed in 1864 by 16 countries.

On 15 October 1914, soon after the First World War began, the Committee set up an International Prisoners-of-War Agency. By the war's end the Agency had handled about 20 million letters and messages and 1.9 million parcels, and its intervention led to the exchange of about 200,000 prisoners. Its card index grew to about 7 million records and led to the identification of about 2 million prisoners. In the Chaco War of 1932 the Committee visited 18,000 Bolivian prisoners and 2,500 Paraguayan detainees.

In 1995 its president, Cornelio Sommaruga, took part in the ceremony marking the liberation of Auschwitz and publicly regretted the past mistakes and shortcomings of the Red Cross towards the victims of the concentration camps.

Its operations rest on international humanitarian law: the four Geneva Conventions of 1949, the Additional Protocols of 1977 and 2005, and its own statutes. Its tasks include monitoring compliance with the Conventions, supervising the treatment of prisoners of war, tracing missing persons and acting as a neutral intermediary between warring parties. It prefers low-key confidential negotiation to public pressure, reasoning that this gains greater access; in apartheid South Africa it was granted access to prisoners such as Nelson Mandela, who later praised it. Its motto is Inter Arma Caritas, amidst war, charity.

The Assembly, of at most twenty-five Swiss citizens, sets policy, and the Directorate manages daily affairs. The Committee had only twelve employees in 1914. In 2005 it adopted the Red Crystal as a protective symbol, and Magen David Adom, which uses the Star of David, was accepted into the Movement in 2006.
international-court-of-justice: The first permanent institution for settling international disputes was the Permanent Court of Arbitration, created by the Hague Peace Conference of 1899, which was initiated by Tsar Nicholas II. It was established in 1900 and began proceedings in 1902. After the First World War the League of Nations Covenant called for a Permanent Court of International Justice, which the League established in 1920. Following a peak of activity in 1933 the court declined amid growing international tension, and the Second World War effectively ended it: it held its last public session in December 1939 and issued its last orders in February 1940.

In 1942 the United States and the United Kingdom jointly declared support for an international court after the war, and in 1943 the United Kingdom chaired a panel of jurists, the Inter-Allied Committee. Its 1944 report recommended that a new court's statute be based on that of the earlier court, that it keep an advisory jurisdiction and that acceptance of its jurisdiction be voluntary. The Charter of the United Nations established the International Court of Justice in June 1945, and it began work in April 1946.

The court has fifteen judges, elected for nine-year terms by the UN General Assembly and Security Council, with five elected every three years; no two may be nationals of the same country, and together they are to represent the main forms of civilization and the principal legal systems of the world. A party to a case that has no judge of its nationality may choose an additional ad hoc judge. Nominations come from national groups of members of the Permanent Court of Arbitration. The court sits in the Peace Palace in The Hague, its working languages are English and French, and a Registry serves as its permanent secretariat.

Its jurisdiction in contentious cases rests on consent, and only states may be parties. It also gives advisory opinions requested by the General Assembly, the Security Council or other authorised UN bodies. It applies international conventions, custom and the general principles of law, and its decision binds only the parties to the case. No appeal is possible.

Among the contentious cases are a complaint by the United States in 1980 over the detention of its diplomats in Tehran, a dispute of 1984 over the maritime boundary in the Gulf of Maine and a complaint by Iran in 1989 after the shooting down of Iran Air Flight 655. After the court ruled in Nicaragua v. United States that the American covert war against Nicaragua violated international law, the United States withdrew in 1986 from the court's compulsory jurisdiction. Rulings are binding, but the court has no formal enforcement mechanism, and enforcement rests with the Security Council, where the five permanent members hold a veto.
international-monetary-fund: During the Great Depression countries sharply raised barriers to trade in an attempt to improve their failing economies. This led to the devaluation of national currencies and a decline in world trade, and the breakdown of international monetary cooperation created a need for oversight. Representatives of 45 governments met at the Bretton Woods Conference in the Mount Washington Hotel in Bretton Woods, New Hampshire, to discuss a framework for postwar international economic cooperation and how to rebuild Europe. The Fund was established there in July 1944, on the ideas of Harry Dexter White and John Maynard Keynes.

For its first three decades the Fund oversaw the Bretton Woods system of fixed exchange rate arrangements. Countries that joined between 1945 and 1971 agreed to keep their exchange rates at levels that could be adjusted only to correct a fundamental disequilibrium in the balance of payments, and only with the Fund's agreement. Special drawing rights, created in 1969, were each worth 0.888671 grams of gold, roughly one US dollar at the time.

After the Bretton Woods agreement was terminated in 1971, the Fund redefined the unit in 1973 as the value of a selection of world currencies, and its role shifted to managing balance-of-payments difficulties and international financial crises. In the early 2000s it provided two major lending packages, to Argentina and to Uruguay.

The Fund is a specialised agency of the United Nations, headquartered in Washington, D.C., and acts as a lender of last resort to members facing balance of payments crises. Through a quota system, countries contribute funds to a pool from which they can borrow, and a country's quota also determines its voting power. Each member has basic votes equal to 5.502% of the total, plus one additional vote for each 100,000 special drawing rights of its quota.

A managing director, who has historically been European, leads the staff, and the first deputy has by convention been a citizen of the United States. Conditionality, the policies the Fund requires in exchange for its financial resources, was introduced in a 1952 decision of the Executive Board. Critics argue that these conditions impose austerity and limit the economic sovereignty of borrowing nations, and that the Fund's governance is dominated by Western countries.
inuit: Inuit are the descendants of the Thule people, who emerged from the Bering Strait and western Alaska around 1000 CE. Anthropologists hold that they had split from the related Aleut group about 4,000 years earlier. They spread eastward across the Arctic and displaced the related Dorset culture, called the Tuniit in Inuktitut. Inuit legends describe the Tuniit as giants, taller and stronger than Inuit. Researchers believe that Inuit society had advantages in having adapted to using dogs as transport animals and in developing larger weapons and other technologies. The Aleut and Yupik peoples generally do not identify as Inuit, and many people once called Eskimo find that term offensive.

The lives of the Paleo-Eskimos of the far north were largely unaffected by visiting Norsemen except for mutual trade. By the mid-16th century Basque whalers and fishermen worked the coast of Labrador and had set up whaling stations on land, such as the one excavated at Red Bay. Inuit do not appear to have interfered with their operations, but raided the stations in winter, taking tools and worked iron.

During the 19th century the Western Arctic lost close to 90 per cent of its population to new diseases, among them tuberculosis, measles, influenza and smallpox. Canadian churches and the federal government later ran the earliest health facilities for Inuit, which involved the forced removal of patients from their communities. In the 19th and 20th centuries Christian missionaries forbade many cultural practices, among them Indigenous languages, dances and tattoos.

Inuit speak Inupiaq, Inuinnaqtun, Inuktitut, Inuvialuktun and the Greenlandic languages. They have traditionally been fishermen and hunters of whales, seals, caribou and other animals. They hunted at sea from the qajaq, a single-passenger boat covered in sealskin that could be righted by a seated person, the design from which the kayak takes its name, and carried people, goods and dogs in the larger umiaq. In winter they watched an aglu, a breathing hole in the ice, for seals. Their industry relied on hides, driftwood and bones, with walrus ivory essential for knives. Labour was divided by gender, but not absolutely. Inuit relied on the angakkuq, or shaman, for spiritual interpretation.
ion-antonescu: Ion Antonescu was born on 14 June 1882 in Pitești, into an upper-middle-class Romanian Orthodox family with some military tradition. His father, an army officer, sent him to the Infantry and Cavalry School in Craiova. He made his name as an army officer in the peasants' revolt of 1907 and in the Romanian campaign of the First World War, when he served as chief of staff to General Constantin Prezan. Between the wars he was military attaché to France and later Chief of the General Staff, and he served as Defence Minister in the cabinet of Octavian Goga and the first Cristea cabinet. His sympathy with far-right politics brought him into conflict with King Carol II and led to his detention.

In the crisis of 1940 Romania ceded Southern Dobruja to Bulgaria and Northern Transylvania to Hungary under Axis pressure, and Carol's popularity collapsed. Antonescu left his assigned residence and negotiated with Iuliu Maniu. The National Legionary State, proclaimed on 14 September 1940, made the Iron Guard the only legal party, with Antonescu as Prime Minister and Conducător and Horia Sima as his deputy. After Hitler told him in January 1941 of the plan to invade the Soviet Union, and judged him the more competent leader, Antonescu crushed the Guard in the Legionary Rebellion of January 1941 and ruled as a military dictatorship. Romania joined Operation Barbarossa and recovered Bessarabia and Northern Bukovina, and he became Marshal of Romania.

His regime's policies were responsible for the deaths of as many as 400,000 people, mostly Bessarabian, Ukrainian and Romanian Jews, and Romani. They combined pogroms and mass murders, among them the Odessa massacre, with ethnic cleansing and deportations to occupied Transnistria. Odessa fell in October 1941 after a two-month siege. The system was inconsistent: it put plunder before killing, treated most Jews of the Old Kingdom with leniency, and in the end refused the Final Solution.

Allied air attacks on Romania and heavy losses on the Eastern Front led Antonescu to open inconclusive peace talks in 1944. On 23 August 1944 King Michael I led a coup against him and had him arrested. Tried by a People's Tribunal in May 1946 for war crimes, crimes against the peace and treason, he was executed on 1 June 1946. The tribunals were comparable to the Nuremberg trials, though the procedures were politicised in favour of the Romanian Communist Party.

Under communist rule the documentation of the massacres came chiefly from Jewish Romanians, such as Matatias Carp's Black Book of 1946–1948. In 2003 an international commission led by Elie Wiesel studied the Holocaust in Romania, and its final report brought official recognition of Antonescu's part in it.
ionian-sea: The Ionian Sea is an elongated bay of the Mediterranean. The International Hydrographic Organization bounds it on the east by the mainland coast from the mouth of the Butrinto River in Albania down to Cape Matapan, on the south by a line from Cape Matapan to Cape Passero in Sicily, and on the west by the east coast of Sicily and the south-east coast of Italy. Its ports include Syracuse, Catania, Messina, Reggio Calabria and Taranto in Italy and Patras, Pylos and Kalamata in Greece. The Calypso Deep, at 5,109 metres, is the deepest point in the Mediterranean, and the sea is one of the most seismically active areas in the world.

The name comes from the Greek Ionion, whose etymology is unknown. Ancient Greek writers, especially Aeschylus, linked it to the myth of Io, who swam across it. According to the Oxford Classical Dictionary the name may derive from Ionians who sailed to the west. Other tales name Ionius, son of Adrias, or Ionius, son of Dyrrhachus, whom Heracles killed by mistake, after which the body was cast into the water.

The sea is known for the seafaring adventures of Odysseus, the warrior-king of Ithaca. It was regularly crossed from at least the 8th century BCE by Greek colonisers founding colonies in Italy. In the Roman period it was the site of the Battle of Actium between Octavian and Mark Antony in 31 BCE. Major naval engagements were fought over its eastern section and its islands throughout the modern era, ending in its control by the modern state of Greece, while the western section has been controlled by Italy since 1861.
ipswich: Ipswich is a port town and borough in Suffolk, on the River Orwell, 65 miles (105 km) north-east of London. It is the county town and the largest town in Suffolk. It was first recorded in the medieval period as Gippeswic and has also appeared as Gyppewicus and Yppswyche. The town centre contains the historic town square, the Cornhill, while the waterfront lies south of the centre on a meander of the Orwell.

Ipswich is claimed to be the oldest continuing town established and developed by the English, with continuous settlement since early Anglo-Saxon times. In Roman times a large fort stood at Walton near Felixstowe, and the largest Roman villa in Suffolk, possibly an administrative complex, stood at Castle Hill. The modern town took shape in the 7th and 8th centuries around its port. From the 14th to the 17th centuries Ipswich was a kontor, or trading base, of the Hanseatic League, with the port used for imports and exports to the Baltic.

In 1824 Dr George Birkbeck and local businessmen founded one of the first Mechanics' Institutes, which survives as the Ipswich Institute. In the mid-19th century coprolite, fossilised animal dung, was discovered and mined, and dissolved in acid it formed the basis of the Fisons fertiliser business. Ransomes, Sims and Jefferies, one of the best-known agricultural manufacturers, was based in the town, and Ransomes built the world's first commercial motorised lawnmower in 1902.

Ipswich has no cathedral, and the Bishop of St Edmundsbury and Ipswich is based at Bury St Edmunds. Among its buildings are Christchurch Mansion, given to the town by Felix Thornley Cobbold in 1896, and Ipswich Minster, once St Mary-le-Tower, rebuilt by the Victorians. The church of St Lawrence houses the world's oldest circle of church bells.
iran: Iran has an area of 1,648,195 square kilometres, the sixth-largest country entirely in Asia. It is one of the world's most mountainous countries, consisting mostly of the Iranian Plateau, with ranges such as the Zagros and Alborz in the populous west. Mount Damavand, at 5,610 metres, is the highest point and the highest volcano in Asia. Lush Caspian Hyrcanian forests cover the north, while the east is mostly desert basins such as the Kavir and Lut deserts. The country lies in a seismically active area, where an earthquake of magnitude 7.0 or higher occurs on average once every ten years.

Hominins were present in Iran around 800,000 years ago, and agriculture appeared some 12,000 years ago; Ganj Dareh shows the earliest known domestication of goats, around 10,000 years ago. Susa, later the capital of Elam, was first settled in 4400–4200 BCE, and Elam lasted from 3200 to 539 BCE. The earliest Iranian peoples began to arrive from Central Asia in the 2nd millennium BCE. The Median dynasty ruled the earliest Iranian state, and in 612 BCE Cyaxares and the Babylonian king Nabopolassar destroyed Nineveh. Cyrus the Great then defeated the Medes and founded the Achaemenid Empire, the largest-ever Iranian state, and his son Cambyses II conquered Egypt.

Alexander the Great conquered the empire in the 4th century BCE, the Parthian Empire arose in the 3rd century BCE, and the Sasanian Empire succeeded it in the 3rd century CE. After the 7th-century Muslim conquest Iran underwent Islamization, and during the Iranian Intermezzo Iranian Muslim dynasties ended Arab rule and revived the Persian language. Seljuk and Khwarazmian rule, Mongol conquests and the Timurid Renaissance followed. In the 16th century the Safavid dynasty re-established a unified Iranian state with Twelver Shia Islam as its official religion. Iran was a leading world power under the Afsharid Empire but lost the status after the Qajars took power in the 1790s.

Reza Shah founded the Pahlavi dynasty after ousting the last Qajar Shah in 1925. The Iranian Revolution of 1979 overthrew the monarchy, and Ruhollah Khomeini became the first supreme leader of the Islamic Republic; Iraq invaded in 1980, starting an eight-year war. The supreme leader is head of state and commands the armed forces, while the president has limited power. Tehran, with about 9.4 million people, is the capital and largest city. Persians are estimated at 51% of the population and Azerbaijanis at 24% in a 2003 estimate, although ethnic composition is debated because no state censuses count it. Iran has 30 UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
iranian-plateau: The plateau spans parts of Central Asia, South Asia, West Asia and the South Caucasus. It is bounded by the Zagros Mountains to the west, the Caspian Sea and the Köpet Dag to the north, the Armenian Highlands to the north-west, the Strait of Hormuz and the Persian Gulf to the south, and the Hindu Kush and Sulaiman Mountains to the east. It stretches nearly 2,000 kilometres and covers some 3,700,000 square kilometres, including most of Iran and Afghanistan and the parts of Pakistan west of the Indus.

Despite its name the plateau is far from flat. It holds several mountain ranges, among them the Alborz, whose peak Damavand reaches 5,610 metres, the Zagros, the Kopet Dag and the ranges of Balochistan. If the eastern Hindu Kush is counted, its highest point is Noshaq at 7,492 metres, and its lowest is the Lut Desert east of Kerman, below 300 metres. Geologically it lies along the suture where the northward-moving Arabian plate meets the Eurasian continent.

Studies of ancient and modern populations suggest that the plateau may have served as a population hub in the expansion of modern humans after their migration out of Africa. In the Bronze Age the civilization of Elam stretched across the Zagros and linked Mesopotamia with the plateau. The kingdoms of Aratta, known from cuneiform sources, may have lain on the central plateau. Archaeological sites there include Shahr-e Sukhteh, Konar Sandal, Tepe Yahya and Tappeh Sialk, the first three associated with the so-called Jiroft culture.

In classical antiquity the region was known as Persia, after the Achaemenid dynasty that arose in Fars. The Middle Persian word Erān, from which modern Persian Irān comes, began to be used for the state rather than as an ethnic label in the Sasanian era. Historically the region includes Parthia, Media and Persis, and some of the earlier territories of Greater Iran.

The plateau holds historical oak and poplar forests, notably around Shiraz, and a wide range of wildlife, including leopards, bears, hyenas, ibex, gazelles and mouflons, mostly in its wooded mountains. The plateau produces wheat, barley, millet, cotton and tobacco, and fruits such as pears, apples, apricots, plums and peaches, while almonds and pistachios grow in the warmer areas. Its timber was used for doors, ploughs and baskets.
iraq: Iraq lies in West Asia, bordered by Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Iran, Kuwait, Jordan and Syria, with a coastline of 58 kilometres on the northern Persian Gulf. The Tigris and Euphrates run south through the country into the Shatt al-Arab and then the Persian Gulf. Fertile alluvial plains lie between and beside the two rivers, which carry about 60,000,000 cubic metres of silt a year to the delta, and marshlands flank the estuary.

Rocky deserts cover about 40 percent of Iraq and another 30 percent is mountainous, with the northwestern end of the Zagros range. Summer temperatures average above 40 °C for most of the country, and most places receive less than 250 millimetres of rain a year.

Iraq largely coincides with ancient Mesopotamia. Sumer emerged between 6000 and 5000 BCE during the Neolithic Ubaid period, and is recognised as the world's earliest civilisation. The territory includes the heartlands of the Akkadian, Neo-Sumerian, Babylonian, Neo-Assyrian and Neo-Babylonian empires. After the Achaemenid conquest of Babylon in 539 BCE, Cyrus the Great adopted titles such as King of Babylon and King of Sumer and Akkad, and Aramaic became the lingua franca of the empire.

Babylon surrendered without resistance to Alexander the Great in 331 BCE, and after his death in 323 BCE Seleucia became the imperial capital in Mesopotamia. Cuneiform writing and temple institutions continued under Seleucid rule. After the Arab conquest in the 7th century, Iraq became the centre of the Abbasid Caliphate, and the name Iraq came into use for the region. The Mongols destroyed Baghdad in 1258, and from the 16th century until the 20th Iraq was governed within the Ottoman system.

Iraq became independent in 1932. A military coup led by Abdul Karim Qasim overthrew the monarchy in 1958, and the Ba'ath Party took power in 1968. The country fought a war with Iran from 1980 to 1988, invaded Kuwait in 1990, and was invaded by a U.S.-led coalition in 2003. Iraq is a federal parliamentary republic.

Oil was nationalised in 1972. The 2021 population estimate was 43,533,592, and most Iraqis are Arabs, with Kurds, Turkmens, Assyrians, Yazidis and others. Arabic and Kurdish are the official languages.
irish-sea: The Irish Sea separates the islands of Ireland, the Isle of Man and Great Britain. Scotland lies to the north, England to the east, Wales to the south-east, and Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland to the west. St George's Channel links it to the Celtic Sea in the south, and the North Channel to the Inner Seas off the West Coast of Scotland in the north. Anglesey is its largest island, followed by the Isle of Man.

The western side is a deeper channel about 300 km long and 30 to 50 km wide, with depths from 80 to 275 metres, while the bays to the east are shallow. During the last ice age the central part of the sea was probably a long freshwater lake, which reconnected to the sea as the ice retreated about 10,000 years ago.

The sea was formed in the Neogene era. In the Roman Empire it was called Mare Hibernicus. Several invasions of Ireland from Britain crossed it. The Norman invasion of Ireland took place in stages during the late 12th century, from Porthclais near St Davids in Wales to Wexford Harbour in Leinster. The Tudors crossed it in 1529 in caravels and carracks to invade.

Because no tunnel or bridge joins Ireland to Great Britain, most heavy goods are carried across the sea by ship. Ferries run from Fishguard and Pembroke to Rosslare, from Holyhead to Dublin and Dún Laoghaire, and from Cairnryan to Belfast and Larne. The sea has also seen shipwrecks, among them the SS Mesaba, sunk by the German submarine U-118 in 1918, and HMS Mercury, which sank in 1940.

The sea lies off Scotland, England, Wales, Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland, and is used for trade, shipping and transport, for fishing and for power generation. Oil and gas fields lie in Liverpool Bay and in the basins of Cardigan Bay and Caernarfon Bay.
irkutsk: Irkutsk lies on the Angara River, a tributary of the Yenisei, 72 kilometres below its outflow from Lake Baikal, about 850 kilometres south-east of Krasnoyarsk and about 520 kilometres north of Ulaanbaatar. The Irkut River, from which the town takes its name, joins the Angara directly opposite the city. The city stands among rolling hills in the thick taiga typical of Eastern Siberia. The Trans-Siberian Highway and the Trans-Siberian Railway connect it to other regions of Russia and to Mongolia.

In 1652 Ivan Pokhabov built winter quarters near the site for gold trading and for collecting fur taxes from the Buryats. Yakov Pokhabov built an ostrog, a small fort, nearby in 1661, and it gained official town rights in 1686. Its position at the crossroads of colonisation, trade and industrial routes gave it a larger role in the history of Eastern Siberia than its military importance would suggest. It became the administrative centre of the large Irkutsk province in 1731. The first road connection between Moscow and Irkutsk, the Siberian Route, was built in 1760, and goods imported from China via Kyakhta, including silk and tea, became widely available.

In 1821, under Mikhail Speransky's reforms, Siberia was divided at the Yenisei and Irkutsk became the seat of the Governor-General of East Siberia. In the early 19th century many artists, officers and nobles were exiled to Siberia for their part in the Decembrist revolt against Tsar Nicholas I. Irkutsk became the main centre of their intellectual and social life, and they built wooden houses with ornate hand-carved decoration, many of which survive. By the end of the 19th century there was one exiled man for every two locals. A fire in July 1879 destroyed three-quarters of the city, including about 4,000 houses. The first train arrived on 16 August 1898, and by 1900 the city had the nickname of the Paris of Siberia.

During the Russian Civil War Irkutsk saw fierce fighting between the White movement and the Bolsheviks. In 1920 Aleksandr Kolchak, commander of the largest anti-Bolshevik force, was executed there, which effectively ended anti-Bolshevik resistance. The Irkutsk Region KGB estimated that 15,000 to 17,000 victims of the Great Terror were buried on the city outskirts, and the burial area was explored only after 1989.

Irkutsk is the largest city and administrative centre of Irkutsk Oblast, with a population of 587,891 at the 2010 census. Its historic centre is on UNESCO's tentative list of World Heritage Sites. The Savior Church, laid in stone in 1706, and the Epiphany Cathedral are among the oldest stone buildings in Siberia.
iron-age: The Iron Age is the final epoch of the three-age system of technology, after the Stone Age and the Bronze Age. The concept was devised for Iron Age Europe and the ancient Near East. Meteoric iron had been used for thousands of years earlier; the earliest known artifacts are nine small beads dated to 3200 BCE from burials at Gerzeh in Lower Egypt.

The beginning of the Iron Age is defined locally by archaeological convention, when smelted iron, especially steel tools and weapons, replaces bronze in common use. Smelting iron requires temperatures above 1,250 °C, impractical to reach commonly until the end of the second millennium BCE, and it also required procedures for removing impurities and regulating carbon content.

The three-age system was first used for the archaeology of Europe in the first half of the 19th century and was introduced to Scandinavia by Christian Jürgensen Thomsen in the 1830s; its name recalls Hesiod's Ages of Man. The earliest tentative evidence for iron-making is a few iron fragments with suitable carbon content from Proto-Hittite layers at Kaman-Kalehöyük in Turkey, dated to 2200 to 2000 BCE. A long-held view that a Hittite monopoly on ironworking underlay Hittite success no longer represents scholarly consensus.

Modern evidence identifies the start of large-scale global iron production about 1200 BCE, which marks the end of the Bronze Age. Anthony Snodgrass suggests that a shortage of tin and disrupted Mediterranean trade about 1300 BCE forced metalworkers to look for an alternative; once tin returned, iron was cheaper, stronger and lighter.

The Iron Age varies by region. In the ancient Near East it is considered to last from about 1200 BCE, the Bronze Age collapse, to about 550 BCE, with the Achaemenid Empire traditionally the end date. Iron working spread through the Mediterranean and to South Asia between the 12th and 11th centuries BCE. In Central and Western Europe the Iron Age lasted from about 800 BCE to about 1 BCE, ending with Roman conquest, and in Northern Europe it began about the 5th century BCE.

In China, writing developed first, so Bronze Age China passes almost directly into the Qin dynasty. Many parts of Africa passed directly from stone to iron, and some archaeologists believe iron metallurgy developed independently in sub-Saharan Africa; the Nok culture may have smelted iron from about 1000 BCE. Indigenous cultures of the Americas did not develop an iron economy before European contact.
isaac-newton: Isaac Newton was born on 25 December 1642 (4 January 1643 in the modern calendar) at Woolsthorpe Manor in Lincolnshire. His father, also named Isaac Newton, had died three months before. Born prematurely, he was a small child; his mother, Hannah Ayscough, said that he could have fit inside a quart mug. When he was three she remarried and left him in the care of his grandmother. From about the age of twelve until seventeen he attended The King's School in Grantham. His mother tried to make him a farmer, an occupation he hated, until his uncle and the schoolmaster persuaded her to send him back to school.

Newton was a fellow of Trinity College and the second Lucasian Professor of Mathematics at the University of Cambridge, appointed at the age of 26. He refused to take holy orders in the Church of England. He served two brief terms as Member of Parliament for the University of Cambridge, in 1689 to 1690 and 1701 to 1702.

In 1696 he moved to London as Warden of the Mint, a post obtained through the patronage of Charles Montagu, 1st Earl of Halifax. He took charge of England's great recoining. He became Master of the Mint in 1699, holding the post for the last 30 years of his life. These appointments were intended as sinecures, but Newton took them seriously, reforming the currency and punishing clippers and counterfeiters. He was president of the Royal Society from 1703 and was knighted by Queen Anne in 1705. He died on 31 March 1727, at the age of 84, and was the first scientist to be buried at Westminster Abbey.

Newton began his work on calculus, which he called fluxions, in 1664, and by 1665 had developed a systematic calculus unifying differentiation and integration. He was self-taught in mathematics. He later quarrelled with Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz over priority. Both are now credited with developing calculus independently, though Newton came to it much earlier. Leibniz's notation, however, proved the more convenient. The Principia of 1687 set out his laws of motion and universal gravitation, and his Opticks appeared in 1704.

Newton was a devout but heterodox Christian who privately rejected the doctrine of the Trinity, and he devoted much time to biblical chronology and alchemy. Of an estimated ten million words in his papers, about one million deal with alchemy. Most of his writing in these fields stayed unpublished until long after his death. His library of 1,752 identified books held 477 on theology and 169 on alchemy.
isabella-i-of-castile: Isabella was born on 22 April 1451 at Madrigal de las Altas Torres, the daughter of King John II of Castile and his second wife, Isabella of Portugal. When her father died in 1454, her half-brother became King Henry IV, and she and her brother Alfonso were left in his care. On 19 October 1469 she married Ferdinand of Aragon in secret at Valladolid. Because they were second cousins they needed a papal dispensation, and the bull produced was supposedly Pope Pius II's, though he had died in 1464.

Henry IV denounced the marriage and in October 1470 declared his daughter Joanna his true heir. When he died on 11 December 1474, Isabella took refuge in the Alcázar of Segovia and was proclaimed Queen of Castile and León the next day. Supporters of Joanna planned to marry her to King Afonso V of Portugal. The war ended in a Castilian victory on land and a Portuguese victory at sea, and by the treaties of Alcáçovas, signed on 4 September 1479, Portugal gave up the Castilian throne and kept most of the disputed Atlantic territories, apart from the Canary Islands.

Isabella tackled the disorder left by her brother's reign and in 1476 created a police force, the Santa Hermandad. With Ferdinand she completed the Reconquista, ordered the expulsion of the Jews from Spain in the Alhambra Decree, began the Spanish Inquisition and financed Christopher Columbus's 1492 voyage. The Granada War began in 1482, and it took ten years to conquer the Emirate of Granada. After a Muslim uprising in 1499, the monarchs broke the Treaty of Granada in 1502 and ordered Muslims to convert or leave.

Isabella withdrew from government on 14 September 1504 and died on 26 November at Medina del Campo. She is buried in the Capilla Real in Granada beside Ferdinand. Of her seven children five survived to adulthood, among them Joanna, Queen of Castile, and Catherine of Aragon. A cause for her beatification was opened in 1958 and she was named a Servant of God in 1974, but John Paul II suspended the cause in 1991 because of the expulsion of the Jews.
isabella-ii-of-spain: Isabella was born in the Royal Palace of Madrid on 10 October 1830, the elder daughter of King Ferdinand VII and Maria Christina of the Two Sicilies. Ferdinand had induced the Cortes Generales to set aside the Salic law, brought in by the Bourbons in the early 18th century, so that his daughter could inherit.

Her uncle, Infante Carlos, Count of Molina, disputed her title, and his supporters, the Carlists, fought over the succession for seven years during her minority. Maria Christina acted as regent, and Baldomero Espartero succeeded her until a pronunciamiento led by Leopoldo O'Donnell and Ramón María Narváez removed him in 1843. Isabella was then declared of age at thirteen.

On 10 October 1846 she was married to her double first cousin Francisco de Asís, Duke of Cádiz, in a union that was unhappy and the subject of persistent rumour. Marshal Narváez dominated the Moderate decade from 1844. On 2 February 1852 a priest, Martín Merino y Gómez, stabbed her; her embroidered dress and corset limited the wound, and he was executed. A pronunciamiento at Vicálvaro on 28 June 1854 led to a popular revolution and the return of Espartero for the progressive biennium. Her later reign saw a war against Morocco in 1859–1860 and the Chincha Islands War of 1865–1866.

In August 1866 Democratic and Progressive exiles signed the Pact of Ostend in Belgium. On 18 September 1868 a pronunciamiento at Cádiz led by Marshal Prim and Admiral Topete began the Glorious Revolution. Historians point to the alienation of both moderates and progressives, the queen's conduct, corruption and an economic crisis. Isabella's forces under Manuel Pavía y Lacy were beaten by Marshal Serrano at the Battle of Alcolea on 28 September, and she crossed into France on 30 September.

She settled in Paris and renounced her dynastic rights in favour of her son Alfonso on 25 June 1870. A coup begun at Sagunto on 29 December 1874 overthrew the First Spanish Republic and proclaimed Alfonso XII. Isabella returned to Spain in July 1876 but was soon back in France. She died in Paris on 9 April 1904 and her body was taken to El Escorial, where she had wished to be entombed. She is the only queen regnant in the history of unified Spain, and was nicknamed the Traditional Queen and the Queen of Sad Mischance.
isaiah-berlin: Isaiah Berlin was born in Riga on 6 June 1909, the only son of Mendel Berlin, a timber trader whose family firm was one of the largest in the Baltics, and Marie Volshonok. He witnessed the February and October Revolutions of 1917 in Petrograd, and a memory of a man dragged from a rooftop by a crowd left him, he said, with a permanent horror of violence. The family left Petrograd in October 1920 and moved to Britain in early 1921, when he was 11. His English was virtually nonexistent at first, but he reached proficiency within a year.

Berlin was educated at St Paul's School in London and at Corpus Christi College, Oxford, and took first-class honours in literae humaniores in 1928. In 1932, aged 23, he became the first unconverted Jew elected to a prize fellowship at All Souls College. During the Second World War he worked for British Information Services in New York and then at the British embassies in Washington and Moscow until 1946.

From 1957 to 1967 he was Chichele Professor of Social and Political Theory at Oxford. In 1966 he helped create Wolfson College, becoming its founding president, and he was president of the British Academy from 1974 to 1978. He disliked writing, and much of his published work comes from recorded lectures, edited from 1974 chiefly by Henry Hardy.

His inaugural lecture, Two Concepts of Liberty (1958), defined negative liberty as the absence of coercion by an external body, and positive liberty as self-mastery. He argued that positive liberty had been used in the 19th century to defend nationalism, paternalism and social engineering at the expense of negative liberty. His value pluralism held that moral values may be equally valid and yet incompatible, so that liberty may clash with social justice.

The Hedgehog and the Fox, his best-known essay for the general public, divides thinkers into hedgehogs, who see the world through one idea, and foxes, who draw on many; he later said he meant it as an enjoyable game. He died in Oxford on 5 November 1997, aged 88.
isar: The Isar has its official source in the Hinterau valley east of the village of Scharnitz, in the Karwendel mountains, at 1,160 metres above sea level. Its longest headstream is the Lavatschbach, and the Birkkarbach, which rises on the Birkkarspitze, feeds the young river as well. It enters Germany near Mittenwald and reaches Upper Bavaria after about 22 kilometres. The river is 295 km long and drains a basin of some 9,000 square kilometres, and at its mouth its average discharge is 174 cubic metres a second. Snowmelt raises the flow each spring.

At Bad Tölz the Isar leaves the Bavarian Alps and passes from its upper to its middle course. It crosses a glacial moraine landscape towards Wolfratshausen, where the Loisach joins it, and then the Munich gravel plain. At Moosburg its most important tributary, the Amper, flows in, and the lower course begins. Beyond Landshut the river runs through the Tertiary Hills of Lower Bavaria and descends some 848 metres in all before it enters the Danube about five kilometres from Deggendorf.

The name is first recorded in 763 as Isura. One theory derives it from an Indo-European root meaning flowing water, which in Proto-Germanic narrowed to the sense of frozen water, as in English ice and German Eis. The river was a prehistoric trade route, and in the Bronze Age Munich was among the largest raft ports in Europe. Between Moosburg and Plattling gold was washed from the river's sediments in the 16th and 17th centuries, though the small amounts found brought little profit.

Industrialisation made the Isar a river of many uses. Since the 1920s its water has generated electricity, and over forty hydropower plants were built on it to electrify Bavaria. In 1923 all the water north of Mittenwald was diverted to the Walchensee for the Walchensee Hydroelectric Power Station. The Sylvenstein reservoir was built between 1954 and 1959 to support power generation and to prevent floods, and it has kept the river from overflowing at Munich in years such as 1979, 1999 and 2005.

The upper Isar is now protected from development. Since 1990 a small share of the water, 4 cubic metres a second, has been left in the river to prevent drought. Under the Isar-plan, carried out between 2000 and 2011, embankments were removed in Munich, the bed was widened, connections to the flood plains were restored and rock ramps were built so that fish can again move upstream. The Isartalverein, founded in 1902 by Gabriel von Seidl, bought 90 hectares of land and maintains more than 330 km of hiking trails.
iserlohn: Iserlohn lies at the northern end of the Sauerland, near the Ruhr, in the Märkischer Kreis district of North Rhine-Westphalia. It is the largest town of the district and of the Sauerland by both population and area. In 1975 it absorbed the surrounding former municipalities of Letmathe, Hennen, Sümmern and Kesbern. Although part of the district, it keeps a special status and performs tasks usually left to the district, such as social and youth affairs, so that it is comparable to an urban district.

The Pancratius church, also called the Bauernkirche, is believed to have been founded around 985. The first written document that mentions the place dates only from 1150. In 1237 the Count of the Mark gave Iserlohn municipal rights, and the checked band in the town's coat of arms comes from the arms of the Counts of the Mark. Above it stands Saint Pancras, patron of the oldest church, between two towers of the historic town wall.

In the 18th century the town became known for Iserlohn boxes, a form of tobacco or snuff box with an engraved or embossed lid that often showed an image of the former Prussian king Frederick the Great. In the Second World War, the tank ace Albert Ernst, born in 1912, is recorded as having saved the town by surrendering it peacefully to US troops.

The Dechenhöhle caves, discovered in 1868 during the building of the railway between Hagen and Iserlohn, have 360 metres open to visitors, with many stalactites and stalagmites. The Danzturm, a tower on the southern hill above the old town, is a landmark and appears on the logo of the local brewery. The Schützenfest, a shooting festival held every year at the Parkhalle, is central to the town's cultural life and identity, and since 1991 a free peace festival has run beside it around the Bauernkirche.

The town is home to the headquarters of the South Westphalia University of Applied Sciences and to the ice hockey club Iserlohn Roosters, which joined the top German league in 2000. Among its twin towns are Almelo in the Netherlands, Biel/Bienne in Switzerland and Hall in Tirol in Austria.
isfahan: Isfahan stands on the plain of the Zayandeh River and the foothills of the Zagros Mountains, about 1,590 metres above sea level and 440 kilometres south of Tehran. It lies at the intersection of the two principal routes across Iran, north to south and east to west. The name derives from Middle Persian Spahān, attested on seals and inscriptions, including that of the Zoroastrian magus Kartir. A Persian proverb holds that Isfahan is half the world.

Human habitation in the region goes back to the Palaeolithic period. Under Median rule it became a regional centre, helped by the Zayandeh River. In the Parthian era Arsacid governors administered provinces from Isfahan, and in the Sassanid era the city was governed by the Espoohrans, descended from seven noble Iranian families. The Arabs captured it in 642 CE and made it the capital of al-Jabal province. It prospered under the Buyid dynasty in the tenth century, and Toghril Beg, founder of the Seljuq dynasty, made it his capital in the mid-eleventh century.

When Ibn Battuta visited in 1327 he found it largely in ruins. In 1387 Isfahan surrendered to Timur. After the city killed his tax collectors and some of his soldiers, Timur ordered a massacre in which his soldiers reportedly killed 70,000 citizens.

The city's golden age began in 1598, when the Safavid ruler Abbas the Great moved his capital from Qazvin to the more central Isfahan. He increased Iranian involvement in the Silk Road trade and forcibly resettled Turkish, Armenian and Persian craftsmen in the city. Industrialisation came under the Pahlavi period, and textile mills earned it the nickname Manchester of Persia.

Isfahan is the capital of Isfahan Province. Naqsh-e Jahan Square, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, lies at the centre of the Safavid city, with the Ali Qapu and Chehel Sotoun palaces and the Shah Mosque of 1629. The Khaju Bridge, built by Shah Abbas II in 1650, is 123 metres long with 24 arches. The New Julfa quarter holds the Armenian churches, among them the Vank Cathedral of 1664.
ishikawa-prefecture: Ishikawa lies on the Sea of Japan coast of Honshu, in the historic Hokuriku region. It covers about 4,191 square kilometres and borders Toyama Prefecture to the east, Gifu to the south-east and Fukui to the south. Its northern part is the narrow Noto Peninsula, which forms Toyama Bay, one of the largest bays in Japan. The southern part is wider and mostly mountainous, and Kanazawa, the capital and largest city, stands on the coastal plain. Other major cities are Hakusan, Komatsu and Kaga.

Ishikawa was formed in 1872 from the merger of Kaga Province and the smaller Noto Province, with its government at first at Mikawa. The seat moved to Kanazawa in 1873. In 1878 six shizoku, former samurai dissatisfied with the Meiji government, assassinated the statesman Ōkubo Toshimichi in the Kioizaka Incident. The national government feared that a Hokuriku bloc might form in support of the Freedom and People's Rights Movement and wished to weaken the former Kaga lords, so it divided the prefecture in two stages. Fukui Prefecture was formed in 1881 and Toyama Prefecture in 1883.

Ishikawa was formerly an important populated centre that held some of the wealthiest han of the feudal period. Noh was introduced under the fifth Maeda lord, Tsunanori, and the tea ceremony came in 1666 when Maeda Toshitsune invited Senbiki Soshitsu of Urasenke to Kanazawa. Kutani ware, Kaga silk, Kanazawa lacquerware decorated with gold dust and Kanazawa gold leaf are among its best-known products. Kanazawa Castle and Kenroku-en, one of the Three Great Gardens of Japan, stand in the capital. Industry is dominated by textiles, particularly artificial fabrics, and by machinery, particularly construction machinery.
isidore-of-seville: Isidore was born in Cartago Spartaria, now Cartagena, to a notable family of Roman Hispania. His family was influential in the political and religious manoeuvring that converted the Arian Visigothic kings to Catholicism. His elder brother Leander of Seville preceded him as archbishop and opposed King Liuvigild, and his younger brother Fulgentius of Cartagena became Bishop of Astigi. Isidore was educated at the cathedral school of Seville, where learned men including Leander taught the trivium and quadrivium. He mastered classical Latin and acquired some Greek and Hebrew.

After the death of Leander on 13 March 600 or 601 Isidore succeeded to the See of Seville, and made himself protector of monks. He tried to unite the peoples of the Visigothic kingdom into one nation. He presided over the Second Council of Seville, begun on 13 November 619 in the reign of King Sisebut, which set out the nature of Christ against the Acephali. At the Fourth National Council of Toledo, begun on 5 December 633, the aged archbishop presided and originated most of its enactments. It ordered every bishop to found a seminary in his cathedral city on the model of Seville's school, teaching Greek, Hebrew and the liberal arts.

Isidore's most important work, the Etymologiae, is the first Christian attempt at a summa of universal knowledge, in 448 chapters and 20 volumes. It is largely a digest of Roman handbooks and compendia and preserves many fragments of classical learning that would otherwise have been lost. His contemporary Braulio of Zaragoza called it practically everything that it is necessary to know, and because it was so highly regarded it superseded the copying of many classical works, which were then lost.

It was the most popular compendium in medieval libraries and was printed in at least ten editions between 1470 and 1530. He also wrote a history of the Gothic, Vandal and Suebi kings and De natura rerum, dedicated to King Sisebut. He died on 4 April 636, after more than 32 years as archbishop, and was proclaimed a Doctor of the Church in 1722.
iskandar-muda: Iskandar Muda, whose name means young Alexander, was born about 1583, the son of Mansur Syah, a grandson of Sultan Abdul Jalil, and of Puteri Raja Inderabangsa, a daughter of the tenth sultan. He thus joined the two branches of the Acehnese dynasty. The Hikayat Aceh, which extols his qualities, describes his youth at length.

Known first as Perkasa Alam, he fell out about 1605 with his uncle Sultan Ali Ri'ayat Syah III and was imprisoned after a failed plan to rebel. When the Portuguese invaded Aceh in 1606 he was released and distinguished himself in beating them back. Sultan Ali died suddenly on 4 April 1607, and Perkasa Alam secured the throne the same day, later having his other uncle Husain killed.

His power rested on a navy of heavy galleys each carrying 600 to 800 men, a cavalry using Persian horses, an elephant corps, conscript infantry and more than 2,000 cannons and guns. He took Deli in 1612, and in 1613 Aru and Johor, bringing the sultan of Johor and his family to Aceh, though Johor expelled the garrison later that year.

He defeated a Portuguese fleet at Bintan in 1614, conquered Pahang in 1617, Kedah in 1619, where the capital was laid waste, and Perak in 1620, and took Nias in 1624/5. In 1629 he sent several hundred ships against Portuguese Melaka; according to Portuguese sources, all were destroyed with 19,000 men. His sultanate kept northern Sumatra but never gained supremacy in the strait.

The economy rested on the spice trade, above all pepper, and he made the court the sole contact with foreign merchants. He suppressed the Acehnese elite, the orang kaya, by forcing them to attend court and barring them from building independent houses, and set up war leaders, hulubalang, and royal officials, panglima, in their place. He created courts using Islamic jurisprudence, and a palace guard of 3,000 women. His rule was brutal: a French visitor of the 1620s reported mutilations almost daily, and he had his own son Meurah Pupok executed, naming his son-in-law Iskandar Thani heir.

Iskandar Muda died on 27 December 1636. He was the last sultan of Aceh to descend in the male line from the founder, Ali Mughayat Syah. Under him Aceh became a centre of Islamic learning, drawing the Sufi writers Hamzah Pansuri and Syamsuddin of Pasai, and the Hikayat Aceh probably dates from his reign. Among the Acehnese he is revered as a symbol of Aceh's past greatness, with the posthumous title Po Teuh Meureuhom, Our Beloved Late Lord.
islam: According to Islamic tradition, Muhammad was born in Mecca in 570 CE and was orphaned early. He grew up as a trader, became known as the 'trusted one' and later married his employer, the businesswoman Khadija. In 610 CE he retreated to the Cave of Hira near Mecca, where he is said to have received the first revelation of the Quran from the angel Gabriel, an event known as the Night of Power. Over the next 22 years he continued to receive revelations.

In Mecca he preached first in secret and then in public, urging his listeners to abandon polytheism. Many early converts were women, the poor, foreigners and slaves such as the first muezzin, Bilal ibn Rabah al-Habashi. The Meccan elite felt he was destabilizing their social order, and they profited from pilgrimages to the idols of the Kaaba. By the time of his death most of the Arabian Peninsula had converted, and Muslim rule then expanded outside Arabia under the Rashidun Caliphate.

The Islamic creed requires belief in six articles: God, angels, revelation, prophets, the Day of Resurrection and divine predestination. The central concept is tawhid, the oneness of God, and associating anything with God is idolatry, called shirk. Muslims consider the Quran the verbatim word of God and hold Muhammad to be the final prophet. His teachings and example, the Sunnah, are documented in hadith. Islam has no clergy in the sacerdotal sense, and no intermediaries are needed to reach God.

Five acts of worship are duties: the shahada, the declaration of faith; the five daily prayers, recited in Arabic and performed toward the Kaaba; almsgiving (zakat); fasting during Ramadan; and the pilgrimage (hajj) to Mecca. The two main festivals are Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha.

The two main branches are Sunni Islam, 87–90% of Muslims, and Shia Islam, 10–13%. The divide began in disagreement over the succession to Muhammad and grew to cover theology and law. Sunnis follow one of four schools of jurisprudence: Hanafi, Hanbali, Maliki or Shafi'i. Sharia, the body of religious law, is studied through fiqh. Sufism, a mystical approach seeking direct personal experience of God, is not a sect, and its adherents belong to various denominations. About 25.6% of the global population, roughly 2 billion people, are Muslims. They are a majority in 53 countries, and about 12% live in Indonesia.
islam-karimov: Islam Karimov was born in Samarkand to Uzbek parents who were civil servants. In 1960 he graduated in mechanical engineering from the Central Asian Polytechnic Institute and began work as an engineer, later taking a degree in economics. From 1966 to 1986 he rose through the Uzbek State Planning Committee, becoming Minister of Finance of the Uzbek SSR and deputy chairman of its Council of Ministers. In 1989 he became first secretary of the republic's Communist Party, after his predecessor failed to quell inter-ethnic clashes in the Fergana Region.

On 24 March 1990 the Uzbek Supreme Soviet elected Karimov the republic's first president. On 31 August 1991, ten days after the attempted coup in Moscow, he declared Uzbekistan independent, the second Central Asian republic to do so after Kyrgyzstan. In the presidential election of December 1991 he received 86 per cent of the vote against 12.3 per cent for Muhammad Salih of the Erk Party; foreign observers and the opposition alleged irregularities.
