A referendum in 1995 extended his term until 2000, and he was re-elected in 2000, 2007 and 2015, each time with over 90 per cent.

In 1999 the Oliy Majlis imposed new restrictions on religious groups, and after an assassination attempt that year the government pressed harder against Islamist movements such as the Islamic Movement of Uzbekistan and Hizb ut-Tahrir. After the attacks of 11 September 2001 Uzbekistan hosted about 800 United States troops at Karshi-Khanabad, which supported the invasion of Afghanistan. On 13 May 2005 troops fired on demonstrators at Andijan, and detailed accounts put the dead at some 400 of 500 protesters. After Western criticism, Karimov expelled United States forces from the base in July 2005.

Western states repeatedly criticised his administration's record on human rights and press freedom, and the United Nations found torture in the judicial system to be institutionalised, systematic and rampant. Karimov died on 2 September 2016, after 25 years as president, following a stroke. He was buried in his native Samarkand, and Shavkat Mirziyoyev, the prime minister, headed the funeral committee and later succeeded him as president.
islamabad: Islamabad lies about 540 metres above sea level at the northern edge of the Pothohar Plateau, at the foot of the Margalla Hills, in the northern part of the Punjab region. It forms a conurbation with the older Gakhar city of Rawalpindi, to its south; the two are commonly called the Twin Cities. The city is 120 km southwest of Muzaffarabad, 185 km east of Peshawar and 295 km northwest of Lahore. It covers 906 square kilometres, and a further Specified Area of 2,717 square kilometres runs into the hills. The southern part is an undulating plain drained by the Kurang River, on which the Rawal Dam stands.

The Pothohar Plateau is considered one of the earliest sites of human settlement in Asia. Stone Age artefacts dating from 100,000 to 500,000 years ago have been found there, among them rudimentary stones from the terraces of the Soan River. Excavations by Abdul Ghafoor Lone found relics and human skulls dating back to 5000 BCE, which indicate Neolithic peoples on the banks of the Soan, who later formed small communities around 3000 BCE. Remnants of Aryan, Soanian and Indus Valley cultures, and Buddhist remains, can still be found in the region.

Later buildings include Pharwala Fort, built by the Gakhars in the 15th century, and Rawat Fort of the 16th century, which holds the grave of their chief Sultan Sarang Khan. The Mughal commander Raja Man Singh turned the village of Saidpur into a place of Hindu worship and built ponds there, and the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb built the shrine of Bari Imam. The modern city was built as a planned capital in the 1960s and established in 1967, replacing Karachi. The Greek architect Constantinos Apostolou Doxiadis drew up its master plan, which divided the city into eight zones: administrative, commercial, educational, industrial, diplomatic, residential, rural and green.

The name means City of Islam, from the Arabic Islam and the Persian suffix -abad. Residential sectors are each identified by a letter and a number and cover about 2 km by 2 km. The city is administered federally as the Islamabad Capital Territory, and its parks and forests include Margalla Hills National Park and Shakarparian. The Faisal Mosque, completed in 1986 to a design by the Turkish architect Vedat Dalokay, was named after King Faisal bin Abdul Aziz of Saudi Arabia, who financed it, and can hold up to 74,000 worshippers. The Islamabad Museum holds relics of the Gandhara period.
islamic-calendar: The Hijri era has its epoch at the Islamic New Year of 622 CE, the year in which Muhammad and his followers migrated from Mecca to Medina and established the first Muslim community, an event commemorated as the Hijrah. Dates in the era are denoted AH, from the Latin Anno Hegirae. In pre-Islamic Arabia a year was named after a major event, and tradition names the Year of the Elephant, in which Muhammad was born, as the year most often equated with 570 CE. The first ten years of the Hijra were not numbered but were named after events, such as the year of permission and the year of farewell.

Muslim authors of the Abbasid era record that the ancient Arabs distinguished permitted months from four forbidden months in which fighting was prohibited: Rajab and the three around the pilgrimage. The Qur'an links these to nasi', 'postponement', which is interpreted as either postponing the month of the pilgrimage or intercalating an extra month. Muslims believe its prohibition was revealed in the tenth year of the Hijra.

The calendar has twelve lunar months and a year of 354 or 355 days. A month begins with the first sighting of the new crescent moon, so it has 29 or 30 days depending on visibility, and the day traditionally begins at sunset. Because the lunar year is about eleven days shorter than the solar year, the months move about eleven days earlier each year against the seasons and pass through them in about 33 solar years.

Twelver Shia Muslims hold that the year's first month is Rabi' al-Awwal, the month of the Hijrah, so that Shias place the battle of Karbala in 60 AH and Sunnis in 61 AH. Saudi Arabia has used the astronomical Umm al-Qura calendar, and the Tabular Islamic calendar follows a 30-year cycle with 11 leap years of 355 days. Most theologians oppose calculation instead of sighting, though jurists such as Yusuf al-Qaradawi have endorsed it.

The calendar fixes the dates of Islamic holidays and rituals: 1 Ramadan, the first day of fasting, 1 Shawwal, Eid ul-Fitr, the Hajj on 8 to 13 Dhu'l-Hijja, and 10 Dhu'l-Hijja, Eid al-Adha. The tenth of Muharram is Ashura, observed by Shias and Sunnis for the death of Husayn ibn Ali. Being purely lunar, it cannot serve agriculture, so farming communities used other calendars, such as the Egyptian and the Iranian.
islamic-revolutionary-guard-corps: The Corps is also known as Sepah or Pasdaran, from Persian words meaning corps and guardians. It was established by Ruhollah Khomeini as a military branch in May 1979, in the aftermath of the Iranian Revolution, and was formed on 5 May 1979 by Abbas Duzduzani. Its purpose was to consolidate several paramilitary forces into a single force loyal to the new government and to serve as a counter to the regular military, which was at first seen as a possible source of opposition because of its traditional loyalty to the Shah. The Constitution of the Islamic Republic entrusted the defence of Iran's territorial integrity and political independence to the regular army, the Artesh, and gave the Pasdaran the task of preserving the Revolution itself.

The Corps emerged from the Iran-Iraq War of 1980 to 1988 as a largely independent organisation on which the clerical leadership relied. Its share of the Iranian military budget was 7.3 per cent in 1980, rose to 20.3 per cent by 1982 and reached almost 50 per cent by 1987. During the war it also built a large apparatus for cultural and media production. Early 1980s reports credit it with establishing over 2,400 libraries, producing some 440,000 publications and holding 4,049 film screenings and 1,620 exhibitions.

During the Lebanese Civil War it allegedly sent troops to train fighters after the Israeli invasion of 1982, and Christian militias such as the Lebanese Forces declared war on it, claiming it violated Lebanese sovereignty. In September 2008 it reorganised from a centralised to a decentralised force, with 31 provincial corps and an autonomous missile command. A command for cyber security was set up within it in 2007.

The Corps is a multi-service force with ground, aerospace and naval branches, the Quds Force and the Basij, a volunteer militia that serves as its auxiliary. Its commander-in-chief is appointed by the supreme leader. Its operations are geared to asymmetric warfare and less traditional duties such as control of smuggling and of the Strait of Hormuz, and it is responsible for internal and border security and for Iran's missile forces. Its aerospace branch controls the strategic-missile force, and its Quds Force trains, arms and advises allied non-state groups abroad.

Its members have taken part in politics: Mahmoud Ahmadinejad, president from 2005 to 2013, joined it in 1985, and a majority of his first cabinet were veterans. It first moved into commerce through networks of veterans and former officials, and grew into a conglomerate with interests across the Iranian economy, including contracts in oil, gas and petrochemicals and in major infrastructure.
istanbul: Istanbul straddles the Bosporus Strait in north-western Turkey, between the Sea of Marmara and the Black Sea. The strait is the only passage from the Black Sea to the Mediterranean. About two-thirds of the population live on the European side and the rest in Asia. The meeting of the Sea of Marmara, the Bosporus and the Golden Horn gave the city both a defence against attack and a natural toll-gate for trade. The belief that seven hills make up the city is a myth: there are more than 50 hills within its limits.

Neolithic artefacts show that the historic peninsula was settled as far back as the 6th millennium BCE. Megarian colonists founded Byzantium around 657 BCE, claiming descent from its founder Byzas, said to be the son of the god Poseidon and the nymph Ceroëssa. The Roman emperor Constantine the Great refounded the city in 324 CE, at first calling it New Rome, and it became Constantinople in 330.

For nearly 16 centuries it served as the capital of four empires: the Roman Empire from 330 to 395, the Byzantine Empire from 395 to 1204 and from 1261 to 1453, the Latin Empire from 1204 to 1261, and the Ottoman Empire from 1453 to 1922. It was important in the advance of Christianity in Roman and Byzantine times. The Ottomans conquered it in 1453 and made it the seat of their caliphate. By 500 CE it had 400,000 to 500,000 people, more than Rome, and it was the largest city in Europe from 1500 to 1750, when London surpassed it. Constantinople remained the usual Western name until the 1930s. The Republic of Turkey made Ankara its capital in 1923.

Istanbul is the largest city in Turkey, with a population of over 15 million. The historic centre is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and palaces and imperial mosques still line its hills. The Galata Tower is the one survivor of the medieval Genoese fortifications of Galata. The first Turkish newspaper, Takvim-i Vekayi, was published there in 1831.
isthmian-games: The games were reputed to have begun as funeral games for Melicertes, instituted by Sisyphus, the legendary king of Corinth, who found the body and buried it on the Isthmus. Another myth, probably later, held that Theseus, the legendary king of Athens, enlarged a closed night rite into athletic games dedicated to Poseidon and open to all Greeks. A further version credits Kypselos, tyrant of Corinth in the 7th century BCE, with restoring the games to their old splendour. According to Solinus they were constituted in the 49th Olympiad; 582 BCE is the date generally accepted, though one recent study places the first games in 581 BCE.

The festival was held in spring, in the second and fourth years of each Olympiad, the year before and the year after the Olympic Games, at the rural sanctuary of Poseidon on the Isthmus of Corinth, a place easily reached by land and by sea. The contests were the same as at Olympia, among them wrestling, boxing, pankration and horse and chariot racing, and there were musical and poetical contests in which women were allowed to compete.

Until at least the 5th century BCE, the time of Pindar, the victor's wreath was of celery; later it was made of pine. A victor might also be honoured with a statue or an ode, and Athens paid its own victors 100 drachmas. Before the games Corinth declared a truce that gave athletes safe passage through Greece: in 412 BCE the Athenians were invited as usual although Athens and Corinth were at war. The games were especially popular with Athenians, while the Eleans boycotted them.

The festival served many as a forum for political propaganda, and from 228 or 229 BCE Romans were allowed to take part. Corinth, rebuilt by Caesar in 44 BCE, recovered the games shortly afterwards, but they were then held in the city itself and did not return to the Isthmus until 42 or 43 CE. Libanius mentions cult activity at the Isthmus into the middle of the 4th century, and the games probably continued at least until the end of that century. The circumstances of their end are unknown; imperial pressure against pagan rites grew at that time, though some polytheistic cult practices continued at Corinth into the 6th century.
italy: Italy consists of the Italian Peninsula, which extends into the Mediterranean Sea, together with Sicily, Sardinia and nearly 800 islands. It covers 301,340 square kilometres, with the Alps along most of its northern boundary and the Apennine Mountains forming the backbone of the peninsula. Over 35% of its territory is mountainous, and the highest point is the summit of Mont Blanc at 4,810 metres. Many parts are of volcanic origin, and active volcanoes include Mount Etna in Sicily, the largest in Europe, as well as Vulcano, Stromboli and Vesuvius. The sovereign states of San Marino and Vatican City are enclaves within Italy.

Lower Paleolithic artefacts dating back 850,000 years have been recovered from Monte Poggiolo. Pre-Roman Italy was inhabited mostly by Italic peoples, along with the Etruscans, the Elymians and Sicani of Sicily, and the prehistoric Sardinians who gave rise to the Nuragic civilisation. Phoenicians established emporiums on the coasts of Sicily and Sardinia, and during the 8th and 7th centuries BCE Greek colonies were founded, an area later known as Magna Graecia. Rome, a settlement on the River Tiber traditionally founded in 753 BCE, was ruled by monarchs for 244 years, and in 509 BCE the Romans expelled the monarchy and established a republic.

Roman expansion consolidated the peninsula, named Italia, and Rome grew into an empire stretching from Britain to the borders of Persia. Augustus, the first emperor, began an age of peace and prosperity. Barbarian invasions led to the decline and fall of the Western Roman Empire, after which the Ostrogothic Kingdom of Italy was created.

By the 11th century Italian city-states and maritime republics expanded, and the Italian Renaissance flourished in the 15th and 16th centuries. After centuries of political division the Kingdom of Italy was established in 1861, following wars of independence and the Expedition of the Thousand. The fascist dictatorship was established in 1922, and in 1946 a republic replaced the monarchy.

Italy has 58,915,561 inhabitants, and Rome is the capital. It has been a unitary parliamentary republic since 1946, with a president elected for a single seven-year term and a perfectly bicameral Parliament made up of the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate of the Republic.
From the late 19th century to the 1960s Italy was a country of mass emigration, and the diaspora included more than 25 million Italians. Italy has 62 World Heritage Sites.
ivo-andric: Ivan Andrić was born on 9 October 1892 in the village of Dolac, near Travnik, while his mother, Katarina, was visiting relatives. His father, Antun, a silversmith who worked as a school janitor in Sarajevo, died of tuberculosis when Andrić was two, and the boy was raised in Višegrad by an aunt and uncle. A scholarship took him in 1902 to the Great Sarajevo Gymnasium, whose curriculum aimed to produce supporters of the Habsburg Monarchy, which he disliked. After Austria-Hungary annexed Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1908 he became involved in South Slav youth movements. In late 1911 he was elected first president of the Serbo-Croat Progressive Movement, and he joined Young Bosnia.

When Archduke Franz Ferdinand was assassinated in June 1914 by Gavrilo Princip, a friend of Andrić, he was in Split, and he was arrested in late July or early August for anti-state activities. Held in several prisons, he spent much of the war under house arrest and was released under an amnesty in July 1917. He studied South Slavic history and literature at Zagreb and took his doctorate at Graz in 1924, with a dissertation on spiritual life in Bosnia under Ottoman rule, which characterised the Ottoman occupation as negative. He entered the diplomatic service of the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, later Yugoslavia, working in it from 1920 to 1923 and again from 1924 to 1941, and in 1939 became ambassador to Germany.

His tenure ended in April 1941 with the German-led invasion. He returned to occupied Belgrade and lived quietly in a friend's apartment for the rest of the war, in conditions some biographers liken to house arrest, writing some of his most important works. Na Drini ćuprija (The Bridge on the Drina) appeared in March 1945, followed by Travnička hronika that September and Gospođica that November. The first chronicles the Mehmed Paša Sokolović Bridge and the town of Višegrad from the 16th century until the outbreak of the First World War; the second follows a French diplomat in Bosnia during the Napoleonic Wars.

On 26 October 1961 the Swedish Academy awarded Andrić the Nobel Prize in Literature, citing the epic force with which he traced themes and depicted human destinies drawn from his country's history. He gave all the prize money, some 30 million dinars, to buy library books in Bosnia and Herzegovina. He died in Belgrade on 13 March 1975. The apartment where he spent the war became a museum, and the Ivo Andrić Foundation supports study of his work. As Yugoslavia's only Nobel laureate in literature he was widely respected there, and Serbia regards him highly, while Bosniak critics have disparaged his works for their supposed anti-Muslim bias.
ivory-coast: Portuguese merchant-explorers of the 15th and 16th centuries divided the west coast of Africa into four coasts named for the trade each offered. The Costa do Marfim, translated into French as Côte d'Ivoire, took its name from the export of ivory, as the Gold Coast and the Slave Coast did from theirs. Other names for the stretch included the Côte de Dents, the Coast of Teeth, and the Windward Coast. In the 19th century usage settled on Côte d'Ivoire, a name kept through French rule and independence in 1960.

The first human presence is hard to determine, since remains are poorly preserved in the humid climate, though polished axes and tool fragments suggest a large presence in the Upper Paleolithic period or at least the Neolithic. Historians believe the earliest inhabitants were displaced or absorbed by the ancestors of the present peoples, who migrated south into the area before the 16th century.

The first recorded history comes from the chronicles of Berber traders, who ran a caravan trade across the Sahara in salt, slaves and gold. Around the southern terminals of those routes, Djenné, Gao and Timbuktu, the great Sudanic empires developed, and they also became centres of Islamic education. From the 11th century Islam spread south into the north of what is now Ivory Coast. The Ghana Empire flourished between the 4th and 13th centuries, and the Mali Empire that followed held only the northwest corner of Ivory Coast, around Odienné.

The country was traditionally home to several states, including Gyaaman, the Kong Empire and Baoulé. It became a protectorate of France in 1843 and was consolidated as a French colony in 1893 during the Scramble for Africa. It achieved independence in 1960 under Félix Houphouët-Boigny, who ruled until 1993. Through coffee and cocoa production it became an economic powerhouse in West Africa in the 1960s and 1970s. The capital has been Yamoussoukro since 1983.

Ivory Coast is a republic with strong executive power vested in its president, and its parliament consists of a Senate and a National Assembly. Since 2011 it has been organised into 12 districts and two autonomous cities. French is the official language and about 78 languages are spoken, among them Baoulé, Dyula and Bété. The citizen population falls into macroethnic groupings, chiefly the Akan, Voltaic or Gur peoples, Northern Mandés, Kru-speaking peoples and Southern Mandés. Each ethnic group has its own music, mostly with strong vocal polyphony, and talking drums and polyrhythms are common.
